## [Machine learning techniques](/science/article/pii/B9780128213797000035)

### 3.5.18 Deep neural networks

The extension of conventional [artificial neural networks](/topics/earth-and-planetary-sciences/artificial-neural-network "Learn more about artificial neural networks from ScienceDirect's AI-generated Topic Pages") is deep neural networks. Compared to [conventional neural networks](/topics/computer-science/conventional-neural-network "Learn more about conventional neural networks from ScienceDirect's AI-generated Topic Pages"), there are two main differences that deep neural networks have. It is shallow for conventional neural networks to have one or two hidden layers. On the other hand, there are many hidden layers in deep neural networks. For instance, a [neural network](/topics/social-sciences/neural-network "Learn more about neural network from ScienceDirect's AI-generated Topic Pages") of millions of neurons was used by the Google brain project. There is a wide range of models for deep neural networks, ranging from DNNs, CNNs, RNNs, and LSTMs. Recent studies have even brought us attention-based networks that focus on specific parts of a deep neural network. The larger the network and the more layers it has, the more complex the network becomes and the more resources and more time it needs to train. Deep neural networks work best with GPU-based architectures that take less time to train than classical [CPUs](/topics/engineering/central-processing-unit "Learn more about CPUs from ScienceDirect's AI-generated Topic Pages"), while recent developments have shortened training times considerably (Sarkar et al., 2018).

## [Deep Learning and Semi-Supervised and Transfer Learning Algorithms for Medical Imaging](/science/article/pii/B9780128167182000154)

[2019, Deep Learning and Parallel Computing Environment for Bioengineering Systems](/book/9780128167182/deep-learning-and-parallel-computing-environment-for-bioengineering-systems)R. Mohanasundaram PhD, ... P.S. Periasamy PhD

### 8.6.3 Deep Neural Network

*Deep* is a word we have all been reading for a long time. Let us understand why it is called deep [neural network](/topics/neuroscience/neural-network "Learn more about neural network from ScienceDirect's AI-generated Topic Pages"). The past rules developed for networks such as [perceptron](/topics/earth-and-planetary-sciences/self-organizing-systems "Learn more about perceptron from ScienceDirect's AI-generated Topic Pages"), HNN, etc., worked on the concept of one input layer and one output layer.

But, if it's more than 3 layers, including the output and input layers, then it is called a [deep neural network](/topics/chemical-engineering/deep-neural-network "Learn more about deep neural network from ScienceDirect's AI-generated Topic Pages"). Hence, deep in its rawest form is more than just one hidden layer. In DNNs, every layer of nodes [9] trains on a different set of features based on the previous layer's output. So, the more you go into the net, the more you can advance into it, and the more complex features the nodes can recognize [12]. This is because it recombines and learns from the features of the previous layer. This is what is called future hierarchy. These nets allow complex nonlinear relationships. The major advantage which DNNs hold is the ability of dealing with unstructured and [unlabeled data](/topics/computer-science/unlabeled-data "Learn more about unlabeled data from ScienceDirect's AI-generated Topic Pages") which is actually most of the world's data. Especially in the medical field, most of the data is unstructured and unlabeled. So DNNs are apt for this large amount of data and its processing. See Fig. 8.3.

So, basically, [deep learning](/topics/computer-science/deep-learning "Learn more about deep learning from ScienceDirect's AI-generated Topic Pages") networks can take all the raw, unlabeled, unstructured data, and cluster it, as well as process, to similar forms. A simple example is that deep learning can take a billion images, and cluster them according to their similarities: dogs in one corner, chips in another, and in the ultimate one, all the pictures of a car. This is the basis of the so-called smart photo albums. Have you ever encountered a situation while browsing the internet wherein the website asks you to prove that you're not a bot by choosing a typical type of photos such as street signs, etc.? Yes, that's what the DNN can do on its own. And much more with extremely complicated data, analyzing which the human brain can take as long as a decade.

## [A comprehensive survey on deep learning based malware detection techniques](/science/article/pii/S1574013722000636)

[2023, Computer Science Review](/journal/computer-science-review)Gopinath M., Sibi Chakkaravarthy Sethuraman Ph.D.

### 4.1 Deep neural network

A deep [neural network](/topics/computer-science/neural-network "Learn more about neural network from ScienceDirect's AI-generated Topic Pages") is an artificial neural network that is incorporated with many layers amid input layers and output layers of the network. Sample DNN with n hidden layers ( to ) is shown in Fig. 3. By using [random projections](/topics/computer-science/random-projection "Learn more about random projections from ScienceDirect's AI-generated Topic Pages"), the input size of the large-scale network is reduced with a factor of 45 over 2.6 million samples. It shows the result in terms of two-class error rate as 0.49% and 0.42% for solo [neural networks](/topics/computer-science/neural-network "Learn more about neural networks from ScienceDirect's AI-generated Topic Pages") and ensemble of neural networks respectively [80]. The accuracy of detection does not depend on incrementing the hidden layers. Two and more layered neural networks result in lesser performance than single-layered neural networks.

Droid-Sec makes use of [deep learning](/topics/computer-science/deep-learning "Learn more about deep learning from ScienceDirect's AI-generated Topic Pages") in which results are compared with earlier 5 [machine learning](/topics/computer-science/machine-learning "Learn more about machine learning from ScienceDirect's AI-generated Topic Pages") models like [SVM](/topics/computer-science/support-vector-machine "Learn more about SVM from ScienceDirect's AI-generated Topic Pages"), C4.5, Naïve Bayes, LR, and [MLP](/topics/computer-science/multilayer-perceptron "Learn more about MLP from ScienceDirect's AI-generated Topic Pages") [81] and is designed for [Android malwares](/topics/computer-science/android-malware "Learn more about Android malwares from ScienceDirect's AI-generated Topic Pages"). Implementing a Deep Belief Network (DBN) allows for the creation of the [deep learning model](/topics/computer-science/deep-learning-model "Learn more about deep learning model from ScienceDirect's AI-generated Topic Pages") [82]. In addition, Restricted [Boltzmann Machines](/topics/computer-science/boltzmann-machine "Learn more about Boltzmann Machines from ScienceDirect's AI-generated Topic Pages") (RBM), components, and algorithms are taken into account. Comparing the results to those of more established techniques like SVM, C4.5, and Naive Bayes, the results obtained are more promising.

The features of 2D binary programs are used for [detecting malwares](/topics/computer-science/detecting-malware "Learn more about detecting malwares from ScienceDirect's AI-generated Topic Pages") that use a deep neural network [58]. The whole framework is separated into 3 stages. In the first stage, four various features are extracted from benign and malicious binaries. The deep neural network is built in the second stage with an input layer, an output layer, and 2 hidden layers. The third one is a score calibrator in which the probability of [malware](/topics/computer-science/malware "Learn more about malware from ScienceDirect's AI-generated Topic Pages") files and is measured by translating the outputs of the neural network. Over 4 million software binary files, 95% DR (Detection Rate), and 0.1% FPR (False Positive Rate) were attained in this. Cross-validation-based methods show high accuracy compared to split validation methods.that implies multiple benign samples need to be analysed to produce improved accuracy. A deep learning-based model called Multi-Task Neural Network (MtNet) has been proposed to classify malware [38] where benign and malicious are classified through dynamic analysis. 4.5 million files are trained, and 2 million files are tested. [MtNet](/topics/computer-science/neural-network "Learn more about MtNet from ScienceDirect's AI-generated Topic Pages") attained a 0.358% binary [classification error](/topics/computer-science/classification-error "Learn more about classification error from ScienceDirect's AI-generated Topic Pages") rate and a 2.94% [malware family](/topics/computer-science/malware-family "Learn more about malware family from ScienceDirect's AI-generated Topic Pages") classification error rate based on the results.

## [The impact of pre- and post-image processing techniques on deep learning frameworks: A comprehensive review for digital pathology image analysis](/science/article/pii/S0010482520304601)

[2021, Computers in Biology and Medicine](/journal/computers-in-biology-and-medicine)Massimo Salvi, ... Kristen M. Meiburger

### 1 Introduction & overview

Recently, computerized approaches have been rapidly developing in the field of [medical image analysis](/topics/medicine-and-dentistry/image-analysis-medical-imaging "Learn more about medical image analysis from ScienceDirect's AI-generated Topic Pages") with the aim of providing clinical information, integrating second opinions and minimizing human intervention. An exponentially growing field in computerized approaches are methods based on [deep learning](/topics/computer-science/deep-learning "Learn more about deep learning from ScienceDirect's AI-generated Topic Pages"), with studies showing how deep [neural networks](/topics/agricultural-and-biological-sciences/neural-network "Learn more about neural networks from ScienceDirect's AI-generated Topic Pages") have reached the performance of state-of-the-art methods in almost all [medical imaging](/topics/computer-science/medical-imaging "Learn more about medical imaging from ScienceDirect's AI-generated Topic Pages") fields [1,2].

Deep neural networks are a type of [artificial neural network](/topics/earth-and-planetary-sciences/artificial-neural-network "Learn more about artificial neural network from ScienceDirect's AI-generated Topic Pages") that are many layers deep, meaning there are many layers in between the input and output layer. The deep architecture allows the learning of more complex models compared to shallow architectures, although it also increases the number of important training parameters, such as the number of layers and number of units per layer.

The recent increase in both dataset sizes and computing power have allowed the application of [Convolutional Neural Networks](/topics/computer-science/convolutional-neural-network "Learn more about Convolutional Neural Networks from ScienceDirect's AI-generated Topic Pages") (CNNs) to the specific case of image analysis, which apply convolutions on the input image. [CNNs](/topics/computer-science/convolutional-neural-network "Learn more about CNNs from ScienceDirect's AI-generated Topic Pages") are the most commonly used deep network, and they are trained on either the entire image or on image patches and the important features are learned by optimizing a specific loss function. During the training process, the weights for each neuron making up a neural layer are learned, and once the training phase is completed, the trained network is then used for inference on new images/image patches.

There are many advantages of CNNs compared to more traditional methods. Mainly, it provides the benefit of automatically learning high-level useful features directly without having to extract handcrafted features, and has a hierarchical feature representation, allowing these multilevel representations from a pixel to high-level [semantic features](/topics/computer-science/semantic-feature "Learn more about semantic features from ScienceDirect's AI-generated Topic Pages") which are learned automatically [3,4]. Moreover, CNNs can provide a [semantic segmentation](/topics/computer-science/image-segmentation "Learn more about semantic segmentation from ScienceDirect's AI-generated Topic Pages") by associating each pixel of the input image/patch to a label or class, and there is the opportunity to jointly optimize numerous related tasks together, such as combining both classification and [bounding box](/topics/engineering/bounding-box "Learn more about bounding box from ScienceDirect's AI-generated Topic Pages") regression [5].

While CNNs are a powerful tool for image analysis, there are also some drawbacks. In particular, deep networks are complex with an enormous amount of training parameters and it can be difficult to interact with any single layer within the deep network. Moreover, deep networks in general are sometimes viewed as a black-box that does not explain their predictions in a way that humans can understand [6]. Still, the advantages often outweigh the disadvantages and over the recent years CNNs have become the most commonly used method in image analysis.

A field of medical imaging where CNNs have been extensively used is [digital pathology](/topics/medicine-and-dentistry/digital-pathology "Learn more about digital pathology from ScienceDirect's AI-generated Topic Pages"), in which histology slides are digitized to produce very high-resolution images typically of the whole slide thanks to whole slide digital scanners [7]. The analysis of histology slides is fundamental for cancer diagnosis and grading, typically done by an expert [pathologist](/topics/medicine-and-dentistry/pathologist "Learn more about pathologist from ScienceDirect's AI-generated Topic Pages"), and is becoming more and more complex due to the rise in cancer incidence and patient-specific treatment options, requiring the attentive analysis of a large number of slides for a complete diagnosis [8]. Moreover, [pathologists](/topics/medicine-and-dentistry/pathologist "Learn more about pathologists from ScienceDirect's AI-generated Topic Pages") must often extract a number of [quantitative parameters](/topics/computer-science/quantitative-parameter "Learn more about quantitative parameters from ScienceDirect's AI-generated Topic Pages") that are required for commonly used grading systems (e.g., cell counting, area, length, percentage of a specific cell presence within slide). All of these issues bring about a very high inter and intra operator variability [9] and occasionally a quantitative measure, such as the percentage of a specific cell presence within a whole slide, really becomes only a qualitative assessment which can depend on the pathologist's expertise.

Due to these issues, many computerized techniques have been developed to process the digitized histology slides in all of the three main [computer vision tasks](/topics/computer-science/computer-vision-task "Learn more about computer vision tasks from ScienceDirect's AI-generated Topic Pages"), which are: classification, object detection, and segmentation. All three of these tasks have an image as an input but the output they provide is different. *[Image classification](/topics/computer-science/image-classification "Learn more about Image classification from ScienceDirect's AI-generated Topic Pages")* has the task of predicting the class or type of an object within the input image, so the provided output is simply a class label. *Object detection* must locate the presence of various objects with a bounding box, and subsequently classify the located objects within the input image. *Object segmentation* extends upon object detection in that the recognized objects are located not by using a coarse bounding box but rather by highlighting the specific pixels of the object. Over the years, numerous deep learning [network architectures](/topics/computer-science/network-architecture "Learn more about network architectures from ScienceDirect's AI-generated Topic Pages") have been proposed in the field of digital pathology for classification (e.g., cancer recognition), detection (e.g., mitosis counting), and segmentation (e.g., nuclei and glands identification) in digital [histopathological images](/topics/computer-science/histopathological-image "Learn more about histopathological images from ScienceDirect's AI-generated Topic Pages"). Fig. 1 displays the overall framework of these networks for each of the three previously described tasks. A detailed description of the three network frameworks is provided at the beginning of each dedicated section (i.e., 4, 5, and 6).

Numerous [CNN](/topics/agricultural-and-biological-sciences/neural-network "Learn more about CNN from ScienceDirect's AI-generated Topic Pages") architectures have been proposed in the literature for digital pathology image analysis [10–12]. Over time, deeper networks have been proposed more to exponentially increase the capability of extracting high-level semantic features from histology images [13]. More recently, studies including integrated or fused methods between deep learning networks and more traditional methods of pre- and post-processing have been growing in number, where the pre-processing optimally prepares the input for the network and the post-processing improves the results of the network output. These hybrid frameworks allow a high-level feature extraction by a CNN with the accuracy of conventional techniques. Occasionally pre-processing techniques can be implemented to locate, manage, and reduce typical artifacts in histopathological images, whereas [postprocessing methods](/topics/computer-science/postprocessing-method "Learn more about postprocessing methods from ScienceDirect's AI-generated Topic Pages") are used to further reduce the prediction errors of the network. Network prediction errors occur either randomly or due to the intrinsic limitations of the [neural network model](/topics/computer-science/neural-network-model "Learn more about neural network model from ScienceDirect's AI-generated Topic Pages"). For example, in [classification tasks](/topics/computer-science/classification-task "Learn more about classification tasks from ScienceDirect's AI-generated Topic Pages"), the [spatial interactions](/topics/computer-science/spatial-interaction "Learn more about spatial interactions from ScienceDirect's AI-generated Topic Pages") between neighboring sub-images or patches can be employed to correct the prediction of the network. In detection and [segmentation tasks](/topics/computer-science/segmentation-task "Learn more about segmentation tasks from ScienceDirect's AI-generated Topic Pages"), basic [image processing techniques](/topics/computer-science/image-processing-technique "Learn more about image processing techniques from ScienceDirect's AI-generated Topic Pages") (connected component analysis, morphological operators) can be used along with more advanced or sophisticated methods (deep fusion models) to both exclude [false positives](/topics/computer-science/false-positive "Learn more about false positives from ScienceDirect's AI-generated Topic Pages") and reduce pixel-level prediction errors. Many of the post-processing strategies reported in this review were initially proposed for [general machine learning](/topics/engineering/general-machine-learning "Learn more about general machine learning from ScienceDirect's AI-generated Topic Pages") problems but, as deep learning became the main methodology for image analysis, they were increasingly integrated into CNNs to obtain better and more robust frameworks. Many studies have shown how the integration between pre- and post-processing methods within a deep learning pipeline can allow to further increase the performance when compared to the network by itself [14–16].

The aim of this review is to provide an overview on the types of pre- and post-processing methods that are used within deep learning frameworks for digital pathology image analysis. The pre-processing methods shown here are mainly specific to the field of digital pathology, whereas the majority of the post-processing methods can be extended to numerous other medical imaging fields.

The outline of this review is as follows. Section 2 presents an overview of the characteristics and challenges in digital pathology. Section 3 describes the common pre-processing strategies adopted by deep learning frameworks for [histological image](/topics/computer-science/histological-image "Learn more about histological image from ScienceDirect's AI-generated Topic Pages") analysis. An exhaustive description of the general post-processing approaches used for classification, detection and segmentation tasks is provided in Sections 4, 5 and 6, respectively. A discussion on the methods and future perspectives of hybrid deep learning frameworks concludes the paper.

## [Algorithm and hardware codesign of sparse binary network on-chip](/science/article/pii/B9780323857833000168)

[2022, Deep Learning on Edge Computing Devices](/book/9780323857833/deep-learning-on-edge-computing-devices)Xichuan Zhou, ... Ji Liu

### Abstract

Differently from last chapter, which focuses on the [hardware accelerators](/topics/computer-science/hardware-accelerator "Learn more about hardware accelerators from ScienceDirect's AI-generated Topic Pages") design, in this chapter, we concentrate on algorithm and hardware codesign. Deep [neural networks](/topics/physics-and-astronomy/neural-network "Learn more about neural networks from ScienceDirect's AI-generated Topic Pages") are the state-of-the-art models for understanding the content of images and videos. However, implementing deep neural networks in embedded systems is a challenging task, e.g., a typical deep [neural network](/topics/computer-science/neural-network "Learn more about neural network from ScienceDirect's AI-generated Topic Pages") can exhaust gigabytes of memory and result in bandwidth and [computational bottlenecks](/topics/computer-science/computational-bottleneck "Learn more about computational bottlenecks from ScienceDirect's AI-generated Topic Pages"). To address this challenge, in this chapter, we present an algorithm and hardware codesign for efficient deep [neural computation](/topics/computer-science/neural-computation "Learn more about neural computation from ScienceDirect's AI-generated Topic Pages"). We propose a hardware-oriented [deep learning algorithm](/topics/computer-science/deep-learning "Learn more about deep learning algorithm from ScienceDirect's AI-generated Topic Pages"), named the Deep Adaptive Network, to explore the [sparsity](/topics/engineering/sparsity "Learn more about sparsity from ScienceDirect's AI-generated Topic Pages") of neural connections. By adaptively removing the majority of neural connections and robustly representing the reserved connections using binary integers the proposed algorithm can save up to 99.9% memory utility and [computational resources](/topics/computer-science/computational-resource "Learn more about computational resources from ScienceDirect's AI-generated Topic Pages") without undermining [classification accuracy](/topics/engineering/classification-accuracy "Learn more about classification accuracy from ScienceDirect's AI-generated Topic Pages"). An efficient sparse-mapping-memory-based hardware architecture is proposed to fully take advantage of the algorithmic optimization. Differently from the traditional [Von Neumann architecture](/topics/computer-science/von-neumann-architecture "Learn more about Von Neumann architecture from ScienceDirect's AI-generated Topic Pages"), the Deep-Adaptive-Network-on-Chip (DANoC) brings communication and computation in [close proximity](/topics/computer-science/close-proximity "Learn more about close proximity from ScienceDirect's AI-generated Topic Pages") to avoid power-hungry parameter transfers between on-board memory and on-chip computational units. Experiments over different [image classification](/topics/computer-science/image-classification "Learn more about image classification from ScienceDirect's AI-generated Topic Pages") benchmarks show that the [DANoC system](/topics/engineering/system-on-chip "Learn more about DANoC system from ScienceDirect's AI-generated Topic Pages") achieves competitively high accuracy and efficiency in comparison with the state-of-the-art approaches.1

## [Machine learning techniques in emerging cloud computing integrated paradigms: A survey and taxonomy](/science/article/pii/S1084804522000765)

[2022, Journal of Network and Computer Applications](/journal/journal-of-network-and-computer-applications)Dinesh Soni, Neetesh Kumar

### 3.4 Deep Neural Network (Deep Learning)

According to Wang et al. (2020), *“Deep* *[Neural Network](/topics/computer-science/neural-network "Learn more about Neural Network from ScienceDirect's AI-generated Topic Pages")* *(DNN) is a powerful class of* *[ML](/topics/computer-science/machine-learning "Learn more about ML from ScienceDirect's AI-generated Topic Pages")* *that stack several layers of* *[neural network](/topics/computer-science/neural-network "Learn more about neural network from ScienceDirect's AI-generated Topic Pages")* *models together”.* It consists of many layers, which connect neurons to solve a complex mathematical function. The input is processed by one layer, and it generates outputs for the next layer. The DNN are dense neural network, [Recurrent Neural Network](/topics/engineering/recurrent-neural-network "Learn more about Recurrent Neural Network from ScienceDirect's AI-generated Topic Pages") (RNN), Long Short-Term Memory (LSTM), [Convolutional Neural Networks](/topics/computer-science/convolutional-neural-network "Learn more about Convolutional Neural Networks from ScienceDirect's AI-generated Topic Pages") (CNN), Auto-encoder, [Extreme Learning Machine](/topics/engineering/extreme-learning-machine "Learn more about Extreme Learning Machine from ScienceDirect's AI-generated Topic Pages") (ELM), [Generative Adversarial Network](/topics/computer-science/generative-adversarial-networks "Learn more about Generative Adversarial Network from ScienceDirect's AI-generated Topic Pages") (GAN), [Transfer Learning](/topics/engineering/transfer-learning "Learn more about Transfer Learning from ScienceDirect's AI-generated Topic Pages") (TL) etc. Dense neural network contains an input neuron with weights and an output neuron with an activation function (Wang et al., 2020). The input features are processed layer by layer across the network, with no direct link between non-consecutive layers in dense neural network. In [RNN](/topics/engineering/recurrent-neural-network "Learn more about RNN from ScienceDirect's AI-generated Topic Pages"), the output at a given time step is determined by both the current and previous inputs (Wang et al., 2020). It contains a “memory” element that stores all necessary data about the operations. In the [LSTM](/topics/computer-science/long-short-term-memory-network "Learn more about LSTM from ScienceDirect's AI-generated Topic Pages"), a variable-length sequence is analyzed by progressively placing the new content into a single memory location (Wang et al., 2020). The gates (activation function layers) control the amount of information that forgot the irrelevant old information. LSTM also solves the long-term dependency issue present in RNN (Wang et al., 2020). [CNN](/topics/computer-science/convolutional-neural-network "Learn more about CNN from ScienceDirect's AI-generated Topic Pages") is a feed-forward-NN that consists of different [convolutional layers](/topics/computer-science/convolutional-layer "Learn more about convolutional layers from ScienceDirect's AI-generated Topic Pages") stacked on top of one another, each capable of recognizing specific patterns in images (Wang et al., 2020). Auto-Encoder (AE) is a DNN that includes both an encoder and a decoder stage (Yang et al., 2018). The AE generates a latent representation, which is used as an input parameter for the subsequent auto-encoder layer. ELM is a generalized single-hidden-layer feedforward-NN with randomly generated hidden [node parameters](/topics/computer-science/parameter-node "Learn more about node parameters from ScienceDirect's AI-generated Topic Pages") (input weights) and analytically obtained output weights (Wang et al., 2020). [Generative models](/topics/computer-science/generative-model "Learn more about Generative models from ScienceDirect's AI-generated Topic Pages") are used to model implicitly or explicitly underlying inputs and outputs distributions (Wang et al., 2020). The Generative Adversarial Network (GAN) is a implicit generative model that determines the probable distribution of real-world data samples and generates new samples from it (Wang et al., 2020). Transfer learning is an approach that aims to use information from one particular domain for assisting learning in a different domain. Some other key [deep learning](/topics/computer-science/deep-learning "Learn more about deep learning from ScienceDirect's AI-generated Topic Pages") algorithms are Restricted [Boltzmann](/topics/engineering/boltzmann-equation "Learn more about Boltzmann from ScienceDirect's AI-generated Topic Pages") Machine (RBM), [Deep Belief Network](/topics/engineering/deep-belief-network "Learn more about Deep Belief Network from ScienceDirect's AI-generated Topic Pages") (DBN) (Ahmed et al., 2021), etc. The Restricted Boltzmann Machine(RBM) is a generative-stochastic RNN capable of learning a probability-distribution from [input information](/topics/computer-science/input-information "Learn more about input information from ScienceDirect's AI-generated Topic Pages") that consists of several visible and binary hidden units layers. The Deep Belief Network (DBN) contains stacked modules of [RBM](/topics/computer-science/boltzmann-machine "Learn more about RBM from ScienceDirect's AI-generated Topic Pages") as middle layers and a classifier at the output layer.

[2020, Journal of Biomedical Informatics](/journal/journal-of-biomedical-informatics)Aakansha Gupta, Rahul Katarya

### 3.7 Deep Neural Network:

A standard [neural network](/topics/computer-science/neural-network "Learn more about neural network from ScienceDirect's AI-generated Topic Pages") (NN) consists of many simple, connected neurons, whereas Deep Neural Network(DNN) employs a deep architecture in NNs with a certain level of complexity and an increased number of layers in a single layer [48,49]. In the past few years, Deep Neural Networks (DNNs) have gained much popularity in [text classification](/topics/mathematics/text-classification "Learn more about text classification from ScienceDirect's AI-generated Topic Pages"). DNN classifiers outperform every other conventional classifier experimented such as IB1-k-Nearest Neighbor, J48-Decision Tree, LR, and [SVM](/topics/biochemistry-genetics-and-molecular-biology/support-vector-machine "Learn more about SVM from ScienceDirect's AI-generated Topic Pages") when tweets were classified as personal and non– personal health experience tweets [33]. [CNNs](/topics/computer-science/convolutional-neural-network "Learn more about CNNs from ScienceDirect's AI-generated Topic Pages") have achieved remarkable performance in computer vision and [deep learning](/topics/mathematics/deep-learning "Learn more about deep learning from ScienceDirect's AI-generated Topic Pages"). It is a class of Neural Network that is proven very useful in the areas of text processing, image recognition, and classification. Recently, CNNs are actively exploited for text classification in the health domain. J. Du, L. Tang, Y. Xiang et al. have also used different types of DNN, i.e., Convolutional Neural Network (CNN) and Bidirectional Long Short-Term Memory (Bi-LSTM), along with other [machine learning](/topics/computer-science/machine-learning "Learn more about machine learning from ScienceDirect's AI-generated Topic Pages") approaches for measles-related tweet [classification tasks](/topics/computer-science/classification-task "Learn more about classification tasks from ScienceDirect's AI-generated Topic Pages"), where CNN has shown a remarkable performance [50]. To study the prediction of [chickenpox](/topics/pharmacology-toxicology-and-pharmaceutical-science/chickenpox "Learn more about chickenpox from ScienceDirect's AI-generated Topic Pages") and eliminate delays in disease reporting of existing surveillance systems, S. Chae, S. Kwon and D. Lee [51] optimized parameters of DNN and LSTM (a special kind of RNN) algorithms.

### 7.2 Deep neural network (DNN)

The deep [neural network](/topics/computer-science/neural-network "Learn more about neural network from ScienceDirect's AI-generated Topic Pages") is a special artificial neuron system capable of classification and generalization. We can consider [deep learning](/topics/computer-science/deep-learning "Learn more about deep learning from ScienceDirect's AI-generated Topic Pages") as a generalization of a human in the sense that there are several layers of human neurons [13]. And just as a human brain is able to recognize a specific image and distinguish it from another image, a deep neural network can learn a model that can identify similar images and classify them. Like the human brain, a deep neural network uses an artificial sensory input, a vector. We provide this input as a matrix called the input layer or also the hidden layer; that is why deep learning is also called a deep neural network. This is why deep learning can learn very complex things like images or characters or speech, whereas a [linear classifier](/topics/computer-science/linear-classifier "Learn more about linear classifier from ScienceDirect's AI-generated Topic Pages") can only learn linear classifications. The deep networking will fasten the 6G advanced communication system. With the help of advanced networking, we can also rebuild neural networks to accelerate the decision-making process.

### Deep neural network.

Deep [neural network](/topics/computer-science/neural-network "Learn more about neural network from ScienceDirect's AI-generated Topic Pages") trained by using a large sets of labeled data to perform [classification tasks](/topics/computer-science/classification-task "Learn more about classification tasks from ScienceDirect's AI-generated Topic Pages") or regression from any types of data sets. DNN includes [Convolutional Neural Network](/topics/computer-science/convolutional-neural-network "Learn more about Convolutional Neural Network from ScienceDirect's AI-generated Topic Pages") (CNN), [Recurrent Neural Network](/topics/computer-science/recurrent-neural-network "Learn more about Recurrent Neural Network from ScienceDirect's AI-generated Topic Pages") (RNN), Long Short-Term Memory (LSTM), [Generative Adversarial Networks](/topics/computer-science/generative-adversarial-networks "Learn more about Generative Adversarial Networks from ScienceDirect's AI-generated Topic Pages") (GAN) and Deep Belief Networks (DBN). [CNN](/topics/computer-science/convolutional-neural-network "Learn more about CNN from ScienceDirect's AI-generated Topic Pages") is a NN algorithm using [convolution layer](/topics/computer-science/convolution-layer "Learn more about convolution layer from ScienceDirect's AI-generated Topic Pages"). Despite the most use of CNN in the object detection field, Li et al. proposed a four-layer CNN-based model to solve the scheduling problem in [Fog computing](/topics/computer-science/fog-computing "Learn more about Fog computing from ScienceDirect's AI-generated Topic Pages") (Li et al., 2019c). RNN was actually created to process trail signals. These networks have a type of memory that records the information. In fact, RNN learn to use the past information. Chen et al. applied hidden Markov model based on kernel Bayes rule and RNN to predict the traffic volumes (Chen et al., 2016). [LSTM](/topics/computer-science/long-short-term-memory-network "Learn more about LSTM from ScienceDirect's AI-generated Topic Pages") is special type of RNN that have the ability to learn long-term dependencies. Yuan et al. proposed dynamic virtual Edge node placement for Edge [cloud systems](/topics/computer-science/cloud-system "Learn more about cloud systems from ScienceDirect's AI-generated Topic Pages") in a mobile environment. With the help of LSTM, the service requests of end-users, and the resource prices were predicted (Yuan et al., 2020). DBN was introduced by Hinton. The proposed network has made significant progress in deep learning. DBN is a potential [generator model](/topics/computer-science/model-generator "Learn more about generator model from ScienceDirect's AI-generated Topic Pages") that distributes shared probability on observable data and tags. A DBN first uses an efficient greedy learning strategy layer by layer for deep initialization (parameters) of the deep network, and then carefully adjusts all the weights together with the expected outputs (Zhang et al., 2016). Alalawi et al. proposed an efficient [ML](/topics/computer-science/machine-learning "Learn more about ML from ScienceDirect's AI-generated Topic Pages") model for [computation offloading](/topics/computer-science/computation-offloading "Learn more about computation offloading from ScienceDirect's AI-generated Topic Pages") in Edge/Cloud environment. DBN and logistic regression suggested for classification phase in proposed model (Alelaiwi, 2019). [GAN](/topics/computer-science/generative-adversarial-networks "Learn more about GAN from ScienceDirect's AI-generated Topic Pages") is an approach to generate new model from the original data set. Wu et al. predicted the future trajectories of mobile users in [Edge computing](/topics/computer-science/edge-computing "Learn more about Edge computing from ScienceDirect's AI-generated Topic Pages") based on the GAN algorithm with the aim of [task offloading](/topics/computer-science/task-offloading "Learn more about task offloading from ScienceDirect's AI-generated Topic Pages") in [mobile Edge computing](/topics/computer-science/multi-access-edge-computing "Learn more about mobile Edge computing from ScienceDirect's AI-generated Topic Pages") environments (Wu et al., 2019).

# Deep Neural Network: What is it and how is it working?

* 28 Mar 2023

-

4

min read

-

* [Data Science](https://datascientest.com/en/category/data-science)

The Deep Neural Network imitates the functioning of the human brain. Find out everything you need to know about it: definition, functioning, use cases, training.A neural network is a **set of algorithms** inspired by the human brain. The goal of this technology is to simulate the activity of the human brain, and more specifically the recognition of patterns and the transmission of information between the different layers of neural connections.A Deep Neural Network has **one particularity**: it is composed of at least two layers. This allows it to process data in a complex way, using advanced mathematical models.

### How does a Deep Neural Network work?

In general, a Deep Neural Network has an input layer, an output layer and at least one layer in between. The higher the number of layers, the deeper the network. Each of these layers performs different types of specific sorting and categorization in a process called “**feature hierarchy**“.

To better understand how a Deep Neural Network works, we only need to observe **how the human brain works**. Rather than learning the structure of the face to identify people, our brains learn from the deviation of a basic face that serves as a model.When we see a face, the brain tries to determine how it differs from this reference model. Features such as eyes, ears or eyebrows are thus reviewed in a fraction of a second.

The differences between the perceived face and the “baseline” face model are quantified by an electrical signal of **varying strength**. All deviations are combined to produce a result.The individual nodes in the system are similar to neurons in the human brain. Each layer is composed of **several nodes**. As soon as they are touched by stimuli, a process is triggered.

The neural network **interprets the data** collected by sensors or directly injected by a programmer. This data can be images, texts or even sounds that will then be converted into numerical values.The different data between the input layer and the output layer must be processed progressively to solve a task or make a prediction. The **first layer** of the network receives the data and performs an activation function calculation to produce a result. This may be a **probability prediction**, for example.

This result is transmitted to the **next layer of neurons**. The connection between two successive layers is associated with a “weight”. This weight defines the influence of the data on the result produced by the next layer and eventually on the final result.

[Everything about Deep Neural Network](https://datascientest.com/en/deep-learning-course)

### Deep Learning: learning from deep neural networks

In order to be able to imitate the functioning of the human brain to classify the data provided to it, a neural network must be trained beforehand. This is **[Deep Learning](https://datascientest.com/en/all-about-deep-learning)**: a specific form of [**Machine Learning**](https://datascientest.com/en/machine-learning-what-is-it-and-why-does-it-change-the-world).During the training phase, the AI is provided with example data. It learns to recognize patterns and features.

When it receives new, unlabeled data, the artificial neural network tries to **categorize** it. Its prediction may be correct or incorrect, and it is up to the programmer to correct it if it is wrong. As the **system learns** from its mistakes, its success rate improves until its predictions become infallible.

### What is a Deep Neural Network used for?

One of the main use cases of these advanced neural networks is the processing of unstructured data. Deep neural networks can cluster and classify data stored in a database. This is very useful for organizing data without labels or structure.

A deep neural network is very useful to **automate some human work** tasks. It is used in the field of video surveillance for facial recognition technology. Autonomous cars also depend on this technology.The same goes for virtual assistants like Siri and Alexa, or even the recommendation engines on Netflix, Spotify or Amazon. So without even knowing it, you probably use products based on **deep neural networks** on a daily basis.

Moreover, **Deep Learning** is making its way into every industry. It is being used in the health field to detect cancer or retinopathy. In the aviation field, it is used to optimize airline fleets.The **oil and gas industry** is turning to deep artificial neural networks for predictive maintenance of machines. Banks and financial services, for their part, are adopting it for fraud detection. Little by little, Deep Learning is transforming all sectors of activity.

Deep Neural Networks are the last link in the evolution of artificial intelligence. Originally, Machine Learning was used to **automate statistical models** through algorithms to make better predictions.A Machine Learning model is able to **make predictions** for a single task. It simply learns by modifying its weights with each erroneous prediction to gain accuracy.

Subsequently, artificial neural networks have emerged. These networks use a **hidden layer** to store and evaluate the impact of each input on the final output. Information about the impact of each input is stored and hidden, as well as associations between the data.Finally, deep neural networks have been invented. Rather than being satisfied with a single hidden layer, Deep Neural Networks **go even further** by combining multiple hidden layers for even more benefits.

[Follow a Deep Learning course](https://datascientest.com/en/deep-learning-course)

### What are the Deep Learning frameworks?

There are Deep Learning frameworks dedicated to training Deep Neural Networks. Several large companies and startups have launched **open source projects** to facilitate the training of Deep Neural Networks.

These tools deliver reusable code blocks, allowing the abstraction of Deep Learning logic blocks. They also offer very useful modules for model development.Among the **most popular Deep Learning frameworks**, we can mention the **[open source project TensorFlow](https://datascientest.com/en/tensor-flow-all-about-googles-machine-learning-framework)** from Google, MxNet or the PyTorch library for Python created by Facebook. There are other, more advanced frameworks, like Keras based on TensorFlow or **Gluon** based on MxNet.

### How to learn to work with Deep Neural Networks?

Deep Neural Networks and Deep Learning offer **many opportunities** for companies in all industries. However, it is a complex technology that requires advanced knowledge and skills.To learn how to create and use such deep neural networks, you can turn to **[DataScientest’s Data Scientist training](https://datascientest.com/en/data-scientist-course)**. This program allows you to learn all aspects of being a data scientist.

In the “**[Deep Learning” module](https://datascientest.com/en/deep-learning-course)**, you will learn about the **[TensorFlow](https://datascientest.com/en/tensor-flow-all-about-googles-machine-learning-framework)** and **Keras** frameworks. You will learn all about the different types of neural networks such as CNNs, RNNs and GANs (generative adversarial networks).

At the end of this course, you will have all the skills required to become a Data Scientist and will receive a degree certified by **the Sorbonne University**. Among our alumni, 90% have found a job immediately after the training.All of our courses adopt an innovative **Blended Learning approach**, combining classroom and distance learning. It is possible to achieve this learning in 6 months in Continuing Education, or in 9 weeks in BootCamp. Don’t wait any longer and discover the **Data Scientist training.**

title: Deep learning
content: In machine learning, deep learning focuses on utilizing multilayered neural networks "Neural network (machine learning)") to perform tasks such as classification, regression, and representation learning. The field takes inspiration from biological neuroscience and is centered around stacking artificial neurons into layers and "training" them to process data. The adjective "deep" refers to the use of multiple layers (ranging from three to several hundred or thousands) in the network. Methods [...] A deep neural network (DNN) is an artificial neural network with multiple layers between the input and output layers. There are different types of neural networks but they always consist of the same components: neurons, synapses, weights, biases, and functions. These components as a whole function in a way that mimics functions of the human brain, and can be trained like any other ML algorithm.[citation needed] [...] Most modern deep learning models are based on multi-layered neural networks "Neural network (machine learning)") such as convolutional neural networks and transformers "Transformer (neural network)"), although they can also include propositional formulas or latent variables organized layer-wise in deep generative models such as the nodes in deep belief networks and deep Boltzmann machines.

In [machine learning](/wiki/Machine_learning "Machine learning"), **deep learning** focuses on utilizing multilayered [neural networks](/wiki/Neural_network_(machine_learning) "Neural network (machine learning)") to perform tasks such as [classification](/wiki/Statistical_classification "Statistical classification"), [regression](/wiki/Regression_analysis "Regression analysis"), and [representation learning](/wiki/Representation_learning "Representation learning"). The field takes inspiration from [biological neuroscience](/wiki/Neuroscience "Neuroscience") and is centered around stacking [artificial neurons](/wiki/Artificial_neuron "Artificial neuron") into layers and "training" them to process data. The adjective "deep" refers to the use of multiple layers (ranging from three to several hundred or thousands) in the network. Methods used can be [supervised](/wiki/Supervised_learning "Supervised learning"), [semi-supervised](/wiki/Semi-supervised_learning "Semi-supervised learning") or [unsupervised](/wiki/Unsupervised_learning "Unsupervised learning").[[2]](#cite_note-NatureBengio-2)

Some common deep learning network architectures include [fully connected networks](/wiki/Fully_connected_network "Fully connected network"), [deep belief networks](/wiki/Deep_belief_network "Deep belief network"), [recurrent neural networks](/wiki/Recurrent_neural_networks "Recurrent neural networks"), [convolutional neural networks](/wiki/Convolutional_neural_networks "Convolutional neural networks"), [generative adversarial networks](/wiki/Generative_adversarial_network "Generative adversarial network"), [transformers](/wiki/Transformer_(machine_learning_model) "Transformer (machine learning model)"), and [neural radiance fields](/wiki/Neural_radiance_field "Neural radiance field"). These architectures have been applied to fields including [computer vision](/wiki/Computer_vision "Computer vision"), [speech recognition](/wiki/Speech_recognition "Speech recognition"), [natural language processing](/wiki/Natural_language_processing "Natural language processing"), [machine translation](/wiki/Machine_translation "Machine translation"), [bioinformatics](/wiki/Bioinformatics "Bioinformatics"), [drug design](/wiki/Drug_design "Drug design"), [medical image analysis](/wiki/Medical_image_analysis "Medical image analysis"), [climate science](/wiki/Climatology "Climatology"), material inspection and [board game](/wiki/Board_game "Board game") programs, where they have produced results comparable to and in some cases surpassing human expert performance.[[3]](#cite_note-:9-3)[[4]](#cite_note-krizhevsky2012-4)[[5]](#cite_note-5)

Early forms of neural networks were inspired by information processing and distributed communication nodes in [biological systems](/wiki/Biological_system "Biological system"), particularly the [human brain](/wiki/Human_brain "Human brain"). However, current neural networks do not intend to model the brain function of organisms, and are generally seen as low-quality models for that purpose.[[6]](#cite_note-6)

## Overview

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Deep_learning&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: Overview")]

Most modern deep learning models are based on multi-layered [neural networks](/wiki/Neural_network_(machine_learning) "Neural network (machine learning)") such as [convolutional neural networks](/wiki/Convolutional_neural_network "Convolutional neural network") and [transformers](/wiki/Transformer_(neural_network) "Transformer (neural network)"), although they can also include [propositional formulas](/wiki/Propositional_formula "Propositional formula") or latent variables organized layer-wise in deep [generative models](/wiki/Generative_model "Generative model") such as the nodes in [deep belief networks](/wiki/Deep_belief_network "Deep belief network") and deep [Boltzmann machines](/wiki/Boltzmann_machine "Boltzmann machine").[[7]](#cite_note-BENGIODEEP-7)

Fundamentally, deep learning refers to a class of [machine learning](/wiki/Machine_learning "Machine learning") [algorithms](/wiki/Algorithm "Algorithm") in which a hierarchy of layers is used to transform input data into a progressively more abstract and composite representation. For example, in an [image recognition](/wiki/Image_recognition "Image recognition") model, the raw input may be an [image](/wiki/Image "Image") (represented as a [tensor](/wiki/Tensor_(machine_learning) "Tensor (machine learning)") of [pixels](/wiki/Pixel "Pixel")). The first representational layer may attempt to identify basic shapes such as lines and circles, the second layer may compose and encode arrangements of edges, the third layer may encode a nose and eyes, and the fourth layer may recognize that the image contains a face.

Importantly, a deep learning process can learn which features to optimally place at which level *on its own*. Prior to deep learning, machine learning techniques often involved hand-crafted [feature engineering](/wiki/Feature_engineering "Feature engineering") to transform the data into a more suitable representation for a classification algorithm to operate on. In the deep learning approach, features are not hand-crafted and the model [discovers](/wiki/Representation_learning "Representation learning") useful feature representations from the data automatically. This does not eliminate the need for hand-tuning; for example, varying numbers of layers and layer sizes can provide different degrees of abstraction.[[8]](#cite_note-BENGIO2012-8)[[2]](#cite_note-NatureBengio-2)

The word "deep" in "deep learning" refers to the number of layers through which the data is transformed. More precisely, deep learning systems have a substantial *credit assignment path* (CAP) depth. The CAP is the chain of transformations from input to output. CAPs describe potentially causal connections between input and output. For a [feedforward neural network](/wiki/Feedforward_neural_network "Feedforward neural network"), the depth of the CAPs is that of the network and is the number of hidden layers plus one (as the output layer is also parameterized). For [recurrent neural networks](/wiki/Recurrent_neural_network "Recurrent neural network"), in which a signal may propagate through a layer more than once, the CAP depth is potentially unlimited.[[9]](#cite_note-SCHIDHUB-9) No universally agreed-upon threshold of depth divides shallow learning from deep learning, but most researchers agree that deep learning involves CAP depth higher than two. CAP of depth two has been shown to be a universal approximator in the sense that it can emulate any function.[[10]](#cite_note-10) Beyond that, more layers do not add to the function approximator ability of the network. Deep models (CAP > two) are able to extract better features than shallow models and hence, extra layers help in learning the features effectively.

Deep learning architectures can be constructed with a [greedy](/wiki/Greedy_algorithm "Greedy algorithm") layer-by-layer method.[[11]](#cite_note-BENGIO2007-11) Deep learning helps to disentangle these abstractions and pick out which features improve performance.[[8]](#cite_note-BENGIO2012-8)

Deep learning algorithms can be applied to unsupervised learning tasks. This is an important benefit because unlabeled data is more abundant than the labeled data. Examples of deep structures that can be trained in an unsupervised manner are [deep belief networks](/wiki/Deep_belief_network "Deep belief network").[[8]](#cite_note-BENGIO2012-8)[[12]](#cite_note-SCHOLARDBNS-12)

The term *deep learning* was introduced to the machine learning community by [Rina Dechter](/wiki/Rina_Dechter "Rina Dechter") in 1986,[[13]](#cite_note-dechter1986-13) and to artificial neural networks by Igor Aizenberg and colleagues in 2000, in the context of [Boolean](/wiki/Boolean_network "Boolean network") threshold neurons.[[14]](#cite_note-MV_1-14)[[15]](#cite_note-15) Although the history of its appearance is apparently more complicated.[[16]](#cite_note-16)

## Interpretations

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Deep_learning&action=edit&section=2 "Edit section: Interpretations")]

Deep neural networks are generally interpreted in terms of the [universal approximation theorem](/wiki/Universal_approximation_theorem "Universal approximation theorem")[[17]](#cite_note-cyb-17)[[18]](#cite_note-horn-18)[[19]](#cite_note-Haykin,_Simon_1998-19)[[20]](#cite_note-Hassoun,_M._1995_p._48-20)[[21]](#cite_note-ZhouLu-21) or [probabilistic inference](/wiki/Bayesian_inference "Bayesian inference").[[22]](#cite_note-22)[[23]](#cite_note-BOOK2014-23)[[8]](#cite_note-BENGIO2012-8)[[9]](#cite_note-SCHIDHUB-9)[[24]](#cite_note-MURPHY-24)

The classic universal approximation theorem concerns the capacity of [feedforward neural networks](/wiki/Feedforward_neural_networks "Feedforward neural networks") with a single hidden layer of finite size to approximate [continuous functions](/wiki/Continuous_functions "Continuous functions").[[17]](#cite_note-cyb-17)[[18]](#cite_note-horn-18)[[19]](#cite_note-Haykin,_Simon_1998-19)[[20]](#cite_note-Hassoun,_M._1995_p._48-20) In 1989, the first proof was published by [George Cybenko](/wiki/George_Cybenko "George Cybenko") for [sigmoid](/wiki/Sigmoid_function "Sigmoid function") activation functions[[17]](#cite_note-cyb-17) and was generalised to feed-forward multi-layer architectures in 1991 by Kurt Hornik.[[18]](#cite_note-horn-18) Recent work also showed that universal approximation also holds for non-bounded activation functions such as [Kunihiko Fukushima](/wiki/Kunihiko_Fukushima "Kunihiko Fukushima")'s [rectified linear unit](/wiki/Rectified_linear_unit "Rectified linear unit").[[25]](#cite_note-Fukushima1969-25)[[26]](#cite_note-sonoda17-26)

The universal approximation theorem for [deep neural networks](/wiki/Deep_neural_network "Deep neural network") concerns the capacity of networks with bounded width but the depth is allowed to grow. Lu et al.[[21]](#cite_note-ZhouLu-21) proved that if the width of a deep neural network with [ReLU](/wiki/ReLU "ReLU") activation is strictly larger than the input dimension, then the network can approximate any [Lebesgue integrable function](/wiki/Lebesgue_integration "Lebesgue integration"); if the width is smaller or equal to the input dimension, then a deep neural network is not a universal approximator.

The [probabilistic](/wiki/Probabilistic "Probabilistic") interpretation[[24]](#cite_note-MURPHY-24) derives from the field of [machine learning](/wiki/Machine_learning "Machine learning"). It features inference,[[23]](#cite_note-BOOK2014-23)[[7]](#cite_note-BENGIODEEP-7)[[8]](#cite_note-BENGIO2012-8)[[9]](#cite_note-SCHIDHUB-9)[[12]](#cite_note-SCHOLARDBNS-12)[[24]](#cite_note-MURPHY-24) as well as the [optimization](/wiki/Optimization "Optimization") concepts of [training](/wiki/Training "Training") and [testing](/wiki/Test_(assessment) "Test (assessment)"), related to fitting and [generalization](/wiki/Generalization "Generalization"), respectively. More specifically, the probabilistic interpretation considers the activation nonlinearity as a [cumulative distribution function](/wiki/Cumulative_distribution_function "Cumulative distribution function").[[24]](#cite_note-MURPHY-24) The probabilistic interpretation led to the introduction of [dropout](/wiki/Dropout_(neural_networks) "Dropout (neural networks)") as [regularizer](/wiki/Regularization_(mathematics) "Regularization (mathematics)") in neural networks. The probabilistic interpretation was introduced by researchers including [Hopfield](/wiki/John_Hopfield "John Hopfield"), [Widrow](/wiki/Bernard_Widrow "Bernard Widrow") and [Narendra](/wiki/Kumpati_S._Narendra "Kumpati S. Narendra") and popularized in surveys such as the one by [Bishop](/wiki/Christopher_Bishop "Christopher Bishop").[[27]](#cite_note-prml-27)

## History

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Deep_learning&action=edit&section=3 "Edit section: History")]

### Before 1980

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Deep_learning&action=edit&section=4 "Edit section: Before 1980")]

There are two [types](/wiki/Types_of_artificial_neural_networks "Types of artificial neural networks") of artificial neural network (ANN): [feedforward neural network](/wiki/Feedforward_neural_network "Feedforward neural network") (FNN) or [multilayer perceptron](/wiki/Multilayer_perceptron "Multilayer perceptron") (MLP) and [recurrent neural networks](/wiki/Recurrent_neural_networks "Recurrent neural networks") (RNN). RNNs have cycles in their connectivity structure, FNNs don't. In the 1920s, [Wilhelm Lenz](/wiki/Wilhelm_Lenz "Wilhelm Lenz") and [Ernst Ising](/wiki/Ernst_Ising "Ernst Ising") created the [Ising model](/wiki/Ising_model "Ising model")[[28]](#cite_note-ising1925-28)[[29]](#cite_note-brush67-29) which is essentially a non-learning RNN architecture consisting of neuron-like threshold elements. In 1972, [Shun'ichi Amari](/wiki/Shun%27ichi_Amari "Shun'ichi Amari") made this architecture adaptive.[[30]](#cite_note-Amari1972-30)[[31]](#cite_note-DLhistory-31) His learning RNN was republished by [John Hopfield](/wiki/John_Hopfield "John Hopfield") in 1982.[[32]](#cite_note-Hopfield1982-32) Other early [recurrent neural networks](/wiki/Recurrent_neural_network "Recurrent neural network") were published by Kaoru Nakano in 1971.[[33]](#cite_note-Nakano1971-33)[[34]](#cite_note-Nakano1972-34) Already in 1948, [Alan Turing](/wiki/Alan_Turing "Alan Turing") produced work on "Intelligent Machinery" that was not published in his lifetime,[[35]](#cite_note-turing1948-35) containing "ideas related to artificial evolution and learning RNNs".[[31]](#cite_note-DLhistory-31)

[Frank Rosenblatt](/wiki/Frank_Rosenblatt "Frank Rosenblatt") (1958)[[36]](#cite_note-36) proposed the perceptron, an MLP with 3 layers: an input layer, a hidden layer with randomized weights that did not learn, and an output layer. He later published a 1962 book that also introduced variants and computer experiments, including a version with four-layer perceptrons "with adaptive preterminal networks" where the last two layers have learned weights (here he credits H. D. Block and B. W. Knight).[[37]](#cite_note-rosenblatt1962-37): section 16 The book cites an earlier network by R. D. Joseph (1960)[[38]](#cite_note-joseph1960-38) "functionally equivalent to a variation of" this four-layer system (the book mentions Joseph over 30 times). Should Joseph therefore be considered the originator of proper adaptive [multilayer perceptrons](/wiki/Multilayer_perceptrons "Multilayer perceptrons") with learning hidden units? Unfortunately, the learning algorithm was not a functional one, and fell into oblivion.

The first working deep learning algorithm was the [Group method of data handling](/wiki/Group_method_of_data_handling "Group method of data handling"), a method to train arbitrarily deep neural networks, published by [Alexey Ivakhnenko](/wiki/Alexey_Ivakhnenko "Alexey Ivakhnenko") and Lapa in 1965. They regarded it as a form of polynomial regression,[[39]](#cite_note-ivak1965-39) or a generalization of Rosenblatt's perceptron to handle more complex, nonlinear, and hierarchical relationships.[[40]](#cite_note-40) A 1971 paper described a deep network with eight layers trained by this method,[[41]](#cite_note-ivak1971-41) which is based on layer by layer training through regression analysis. Superfluous hidden units are pruned using a separate validation set. Since the activation functions of the nodes are Kolmogorov-Gabor polynomials, these were also the first deep networks with multiplicative units or "gates".[[31]](#cite_note-DLhistory-31)

The first deep learning [multilayer perceptron](/wiki/Multilayer_perceptron "Multilayer perceptron") trained by [stochastic gradient descent](/wiki/Stochastic_gradient_descent "Stochastic gradient descent")[[42]](#cite_note-robbins1951-42) was published in 1967 by [Shun'ichi Amari](/wiki/Shun%27ichi_Amari "Shun'ichi Amari").[[43]](#cite_note-Amari1967-43) In computer experiments conducted by Amari's student Saito, a five layer MLP with two modifiable layers learned [internal representations](/wiki/Knowledge_representation "Knowledge representation") to classify non-linearily separable pattern classes.[[31]](#cite_note-DLhistory-31) Subsequent developments in hardware and hyperparameter tunings have made end-to-end [stochastic gradient descent](/wiki/Stochastic_gradient_descent "Stochastic gradient descent") the currently dominant training technique.

In 1969, [Kunihiko Fukushima](/wiki/Kunihiko_Fukushima "Kunihiko Fukushima") introduced the [ReLU](/wiki/Rectifier_(neural_networks) "Rectifier (neural networks)") (rectified linear unit) [activation function](/wiki/Activation_function "Activation function").[[25]](#cite_note-Fukushima1969-25)[[31]](#cite_note-DLhistory-31) The rectifier has become the most popular activation function for deep learning.[[44]](#cite_note-44)

Deep learning architectures for [convolutional neural networks](/wiki/Convolutional_neural_network "Convolutional neural network") (CNNs) with convolutional layers and downsampling layers began with the [Neocognitron](/wiki/Neocognitron "Neocognitron") introduced by [Kunihiko Fukushima](/wiki/Kunihiko_Fukushima "Kunihiko Fukushima") in 1979, though not trained by backpropagation.[[45]](#cite_note-FUKU1979-45)[[46]](#cite_note-FUKU1980-46)

[Backpropagation](/wiki/Backpropagation "Backpropagation") is an efficient application of the [chain rule](/wiki/Chain_rule "Chain rule") derived by [Gottfried Wilhelm Leibniz](/wiki/Gottfried_Wilhelm_Leibniz "Gottfried Wilhelm Leibniz") in 1673[[47]](#cite_note-leibniz1676-47) to networks of differentiable nodes. The terminology "back-propagating errors" was actually introduced in 1962 by Rosenblatt,[[37]](#cite_note-rosenblatt1962-37) but he did not know how to implement this, although [Henry J. Kelley](/wiki/Henry_J._Kelley "Henry J. Kelley") had a continuous precursor of backpropagation in 1960 in the context of [control theory](/wiki/Control_theory "Control theory").[[48]](#cite_note-kelley1960-48) The modern form of backpropagation was first published in [Seppo Linnainmaa](/wiki/Seppo_Linnainmaa "Seppo Linnainmaa")'s master thesis (1970).[[49]](#cite_note-lin19703-49)[[50]](#cite_note-lin19763-50)[[31]](#cite_note-DLhistory-31) G.M. Ostrovski et al. republished it in 1971.[[51]](#cite_note-ostrowski1971-51)[[52]](#cite_note-backprop-52) [Paul Werbos](/wiki/Paul_Werbos "Paul Werbos") applied backpropagation to neural networks in 1982[[53]](#cite_note-werbos1982-53) (his 1974 PhD thesis, reprinted in a 1994 book,[[54]](#cite_note-werbos1974-54) did not yet describe the algorithm[[52]](#cite_note-backprop-52)). In 1986, [David E. Rumelhart](/wiki/David_E._Rumelhart "David E. Rumelhart") et al. popularised backpropagation but did not cite the original work.[[55]](#cite_note-55)[[56]](#cite_note-rumelhart1986-56)

### 1980s-2000s

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Deep_learning&action=edit&section=5 "Edit section: 1980s-2000s")]

The [time delay neural network](/wiki/Time_delay_neural_network "Time delay neural network") (TDNN) was introduced in 1987 by [Alex Waibel](/wiki/Alex_Waibel "Alex Waibel") to apply CNN to phoneme recognition. It used convolutions, weight sharing, and backpropagation.[[57]](#cite_note-Waibel1987-57)[[58]](#cite_note-speechsignal-58) In 1988, Wei Zhang applied a backpropagation-trained CNN to alphabet recognition.[[59]](#cite_note-wz1988-59) In 1989, [Yann LeCun](/wiki/Yann_LeCun "Yann LeCun") et al. created a CNN called [LeNet](/wiki/LeNet "LeNet") for [recognizing handwritten ZIP codes](/wiki/Handwriting_recognition "Handwriting recognition") on mail. Training required 3 days.[[60]](#cite_note-LECUN1989-60) In 1990, Wei Zhang implemented a CNN on [optical computing](/wiki/Optical_computing "Optical computing") hardware.[[61]](#cite_note-wz1990-61) In 1991, a CNN was applied to medical image object segmentation[[62]](#cite_note-62) and breast cancer detection in mammograms.[[63]](#cite_note-63) [LeNet](/wiki/LeNet "LeNet")-5 (1998), a 7-level CNN by [Yann LeCun](/wiki/Yann_LeCun "Yann LeCun") et al., that classifies digits, was applied by several banks to recognize hand-written numbers on checks digitized in 32x32 pixel images.[[64]](#cite_note-lecun98-64)

[Recurrent neural networks](/wiki/Recurrent_neural_network "Recurrent neural network") (RNN)[[28]](#cite_note-ising1925-28)[[30]](#cite_note-Amari1972-30) were further developed in the 1980s. Recurrence is used for sequence processing, and when a recurrent network is unrolled, it mathematically resembles a deep feedforward layer. Consequently, they have similar properties and issues, and their developments had mutual influences. In RNN, two early influential works were the [Jordan network](/wiki/Recurrent_neural_network#Jordan_network "Recurrent neural network") (1986)[[65]](#cite_note-65) and the [Elman network](/wiki/Recurrent_neural_network#Elman_network "Recurrent neural network") (1990),[[66]](#cite_note-66) which applied RNN to study problems in [cognitive psychology](/wiki/Cognitive_psychology "Cognitive psychology").

In the 1980s, backpropagation did not work well for deep learning with long credit assignment paths. To overcome this problem, in 1991, [Jürgen Schmidhuber](/wiki/J%C3%BCrgen_Schmidhuber "Jürgen Schmidhuber") proposed a hierarchy of RNNs pre-trained one level at a time by [self-supervised learning](/wiki/Self-supervised_learning "Self-supervised learning") where each RNN tries to predict its own next input, which is the next unexpected input of the RNN below.[[67]](#cite_note-chunker1991-67)[[68]](#cite_note-schmidhuber1992-68) This "neural history compressor" uses [predictive coding](/wiki/Predictive_coding "Predictive coding") to learn [internal representations](/wiki/Knowledge_representation "Knowledge representation") at multiple self-organizing time scales. This can substantially facilitate downstream deep learning. The RNN hierarchy can be *collapsed* into a single RNN, by [distilling](/wiki/Knowledge_distillation "Knowledge distillation") a higher level *chunker* network into a lower level *automatizer* network.[[67]](#cite_note-chunker1991-67)[[68]](#cite_note-schmidhuber1992-68)[[31]](#cite_note-DLhistory-31) In 1993, a neural history compressor solved a "Very Deep Learning" task that required more than 1000 subsequent [layers](/wiki/Layer_(deep_learning) "Layer (deep learning)") in an RNN unfolded in time.[[69]](#cite_note-schmidhuber1993-69) The "P" in [ChatGPT](/wiki/ChatGPT "ChatGPT") refers to such pre-training.

[Sepp Hochreiter](/wiki/Sepp_Hochreiter "Sepp Hochreiter")'s diploma thesis (1991)[[70]](#cite_note-HOCH1991-70) implemented the neural history compressor,[[67]](#cite_note-chunker1991-67) and identified and analyzed the [vanishing gradient problem](/wiki/Vanishing_gradient_problem "Vanishing gradient problem").[[70]](#cite_note-HOCH1991-70)[[71]](#cite_note-HOCH2001-71) Hochreiter proposed recurrent [residual](/wiki/Residual_neural_network "Residual neural network") connections to solve the vanishing gradient problem. This led to the [long short-term memory](/wiki/Long_short-term_memory "Long short-term memory") (LSTM), published in 1995.[[72]](#cite_note-72) LSTM can learn "very deep learning" tasks[[9]](#cite_note-SCHIDHUB-9) with long credit assignment paths that require memories of events that happened thousands of discrete time steps before. That LSTM was not yet the modern architecture, which required a "forget gate", introduced in 1999,[[73]](#cite_note-lstm1999-73) which became the standard RNN architecture.

In 1991, [Jürgen Schmidhuber](/wiki/J%C3%BCrgen_Schmidhuber "Jürgen Schmidhuber") also published adversarial neural networks that contest with each other in the form of a [zero-sum game](/wiki/Zero-sum_game "Zero-sum game"), where one network's gain is the other network's loss.[[74]](#cite_note-curiosity1991-74)[[75]](#cite_note-fun2010-75) The first network is a [generative model](/wiki/Generative_model "Generative model") that models a [probability distribution](/wiki/Probability_distribution "Probability distribution") over output patterns. The second network learns by [gradient descent](/wiki/Gradient_descent "Gradient descent") to predict the reactions of the environment to these patterns. This was called "artificial curiosity". In 2014, this principle was used in [generative adversarial networks](/wiki/Generative_adversarial_network "Generative adversarial network") (GANs).[[76]](#cite_note-gancurpm2020-76)

During 1985–1995, inspired by statistical mechanics, several architectures and methods were developed by [Terry Sejnowski](/wiki/Terry_Sejnowski "Terry Sejnowski"), [Peter Dayan](/wiki/Peter_Dayan "Peter Dayan"), [Geoffrey Hinton](/wiki/Geoffrey_Hinton "Geoffrey Hinton"), etc., including the [Boltzmann machine](/wiki/Boltzmann_machine "Boltzmann machine"),[[77]](#cite_note-77) [restricted Boltzmann machine](/wiki/Restricted_Boltzmann_machine "Restricted Boltzmann machine"),[[78]](#cite_note-78) [Helmholtz machine](/wiki/Helmholtz_machine "Helmholtz machine"),[[79]](#cite_note-nc95-79) and the [wake-sleep algorithm](/wiki/Wake-sleep_algorithm "Wake-sleep algorithm").[[80]](#cite_note-:1-80) These were designed for unsupervised learning of deep generative models. However, those were more computationally expensive compared to backpropagation. Boltzmann machine learning algorithm, published in 1985, was briefly popular before being eclipsed by the backpropagation algorithm in 1986. (p. 112 [[81]](#cite_note-81)). A 1988 network became state of the art in [protein structure prediction](/wiki/Protein_structure_prediction "Protein structure prediction"), an early application of deep learning to bioinformatics.[[82]](#cite_note-82)

Both shallow and deep learning (e.g., recurrent nets) of ANNs for [speech recognition](/wiki/Speech_recognition "Speech recognition") have been explored for many years.[[83]](#cite_note-83)[[84]](#cite_note-Robinson1992-84)[[85]](#cite_note-85) These methods never outperformed non-uniform internal-handcrafting Gaussian [mixture model](/wiki/Mixture_model "Mixture model")/[Hidden Markov model](/wiki/Hidden_Markov_model "Hidden Markov model") (GMM-HMM) technology based on generative models of speech trained discriminatively.[[86]](#cite_note-Baker2009-86) Key difficulties have been analyzed, including gradient diminishing[[70]](#cite_note-HOCH1991-70) and weak temporal correlation structure in neural predictive models.[[87]](#cite_note-Bengio1991-87)[[88]](#cite_note-Deng1994-88) Additional difficulties were the lack of training data and limited computing power.

Most [speech recognition](/wiki/Speech_recognition "Speech recognition") researchers moved away from neural nets to pursue generative modeling. An exception was at [SRI International](/wiki/SRI_International "SRI International") in the late 1990s. Funded by the US government's [NSA](/wiki/National_Security_Agency "National Security Agency") and [DARPA](/wiki/DARPA "DARPA"), SRI researched in speech and [speaker recognition](/wiki/Speaker_recognition "Speaker recognition"). The speaker recognition team led by [Larry Heck](/wiki/Larry_Heck "Larry Heck") reported significant success with deep neural networks in speech processing in the 1998 [NIST](/wiki/National_Institute_of_Standards_and_Technology "National Institute of Standards and Technology") Speaker Recognition benchmark.[[89]](#cite_note-Doddington2000-89)[[90]](#cite_note-Heck2000-90) It was deployed in the Nuance Verifier, representing the first major industrial application of deep learning.[[91]](#cite_note-91)

The principle of elevating "raw" features over hand-crafted optimization was first explored successfully in the architecture of deep autoencoder on the "raw" spectrogram or linear [filter-bank](/wiki/Filter_bank "Filter bank") features in the late 1990s,[[90]](#cite_note-Heck2000-90) showing its superiority over the [Mel-Cepstral](/wiki/Mel-frequency_cepstrum "Mel-frequency cepstrum") features that contain stages of fixed transformation from spectrograms. The raw features of speech, [waveforms](/wiki/Waveform "Waveform"), later produced excellent larger-scale results.[[92]](#cite_note-92)

### 2000s

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Deep_learning&action=edit&section=6 "Edit section: 2000s")]

Neural networks entered a lull, and simpler models that use task-specific handcrafted features such as [Gabor filters](/wiki/Gabor_filter "Gabor filter") and [support vector machines](/wiki/Support_vector_machine "Support vector machine") (SVMs) became the preferred choices in the 1990s and 2000s, because of artificial neural networks' computational cost and a lack of understanding of how the brain wires its biological networks.[*[citation needed](/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation_needed "Wikipedia:Citation needed")*]

In 2003, LSTM became competitive with traditional speech recognizers on certain tasks.[[93]](#cite_note-graves2003-93) In 2006, [Alex Graves](/wiki/Alex_Graves_(computer_scientist) "Alex Graves (computer scientist)"), Santiago Fernández, Faustino Gomez, and Schmidhuber combined it with [connectionist temporal classification](/wiki/Connectionist_temporal_classification "Connectionist temporal classification") (CTC)[[94]](#cite_note-graves2006-94) in stacks of LSTMs.[[95]](#cite_note-fernandez2007keyword-95) In 2009, it became the first RNN to win a [pattern recognition](/wiki/Pattern_recognition "Pattern recognition") contest, in connected [handwriting recognition](/wiki/Handwriting_recognition "Handwriting recognition").[[96]](#cite_note-96)[[9]](#cite_note-SCHIDHUB-9)

In 2006, publications by [Geoff Hinton](/wiki/Geoffrey_Hinton "Geoffrey Hinton"), [Ruslan Salakhutdinov](/wiki/Russ_Salakhutdinov "Russ Salakhutdinov"), Osindero and [Teh](/wiki/Yee_Whye_Teh "Yee Whye Teh")[[97]](#cite_note-97)[[98]](#cite_note-hinton06-98) [deep belief networks](/wiki/Deep_belief_network "Deep belief network") were developed for generative modeling. They are trained by training one restricted Boltzmann machine, then freezing it and training another one on top of the first one, and so on, then optionally [fine-tuned](/wiki/Fine-tuning_(deep_learning) "Fine-tuning (deep learning)") using supervised backpropagation.[[99]](#cite_note-HINTON2007-99) They could model high-dimensional probability distributions, such as the distribution of [MNIST images](/wiki/MNIST_database "MNIST database"), but convergence was slow.[[100]](#cite_note-100)[[101]](#cite_note-101)[[102]](#cite_note-102)

The impact of deep learning in industry began in the early 2000s, when CNNs already processed an estimated 10% to 20% of all the checks written in the US, according to Yann LeCun.[[103]](#cite_note-lecun2016slides-103) Industrial applications of deep learning to large-scale speech recognition started around 2010.

The 2009 NIPS Workshop on Deep Learning for Speech Recognition was motivated by the limitations of deep generative models of speech, and the possibility that given more capable hardware and large-scale data sets that deep neural nets might become practical. It was believed that pre-training DNNs using generative models of deep belief nets (DBN) would overcome the main difficulties of neural nets.
