However, it was discovered that replacing pre-training with large amounts of training data for straightforward backpropagation when using DNNs with large, context-dependent output layers produced error rates dramatically lower than then-state-of-the-art Gaussian mixture model (GMM)/Hidden Markov Model (HMM) and also than more-advanced generative model-based systems.[[104]](#cite_note-HintonDengYu2012-104) The nature of the recognition errors produced by the two types of systems was characteristically different,[[105]](#cite_note-ReferenceICASSP2013-105) offering technical insights into how to integrate deep learning into the existing highly efficient, run-time speech decoding system deployed by all major speech recognition systems.[[23]](#cite_note-BOOK2014-23)[[106]](#cite_note-ReferenceA-106)[[107]](#cite_note-107) Analysis around 2009–2010, contrasting the GMM (and other generative speech models) vs. DNN models, stimulated early industrial investment in deep learning for speech recognition.[[105]](#cite_note-ReferenceICASSP2013-105) That analysis was done with comparable performance (less than 1.5% in error rate) between discriminative DNNs and generative models.[[104]](#cite_note-HintonDengYu2012-104)[[105]](#cite_note-ReferenceICASSP2013-105)[[108]](#cite_note-interspeech2014Keynote-108) In 2010, researchers extended deep learning from [TIMIT](/wiki/TIMIT "TIMIT") to large vocabulary speech recognition, by adopting large output layers of the DNN based on context-dependent HMM states constructed by [decision trees](/wiki/Decision_tree "Decision tree").[[109]](#cite_note-Roles2010-109)[[110]](#cite_note-110)[[111]](#cite_note-111)[[106]](#cite_note-ReferenceA-106)

### Deep learning revolution

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Deep_learning&action=edit&section=7 "Edit section: Deep learning revolution")]

The deep learning revolution started around CNN- and GPU-based computer vision.

Although CNNs trained by backpropagation had been around for decades and GPU implementations of NNs for years,[[112]](#cite_note-jung2004-112) including CNNs,[[113]](#cite_note-chellapilla2006-113) faster implementations of CNNs on GPUs were needed to progress on computer vision. Later, as deep learning becomes widespread, specialized hardware and algorithm optimizations were developed specifically for deep learning.[[114]](#cite_note-sze2017-114)

A key advance for the deep learning revolution was hardware advances, especially GPU. Some early work dated back to 2004.[[112]](#cite_note-jung2004-112)[[113]](#cite_note-chellapilla2006-113) In 2009, Raina, Madhavan, and [Andrew Ng](/wiki/Andrew_Ng "Andrew Ng") reported a 100M deep belief network trained on 30 Nvidia [GeForce GTX 280](/wiki/GeForce_GTX_280 "GeForce GTX 280") GPUs, an early demonstration of GPU-based deep learning. They reported up to 70 times faster training.[[115]](#cite_note-115)

In 2011, a CNN named *DanNet[[116]](#cite_note-:3-116)*[[117]](#cite_note-:6-117) by Dan Ciresan, Ueli Meier, Jonathan Masci, [Luca Maria Gambardella](/wiki/Luca_Maria_Gambardella "Luca Maria Gambardella"), and [Jürgen Schmidhuber](/wiki/J%C3%BCrgen_Schmidhuber "Jürgen Schmidhuber") achieved for the first time superhuman performance in a visual pattern recognition contest, outperforming traditional methods by a factor of 3.[[9]](#cite_note-SCHIDHUB-9) It then won more contests.[[118]](#cite_note-:8-118)[[119]](#cite_note-ciresan2013miccai-119) They also showed how [max-pooling](/wiki/Max_pooling "Max pooling") CNNs on GPU improved performance significantly.[[3]](#cite_note-:9-3)

In 2012, [Andrew Ng](/wiki/Andrew_Ng "Andrew Ng") and [Jeff Dean](/wiki/Jeff_Dean_(computer_scientist) "Jeff Dean (computer scientist)") created an FNN that learned to recognize higher-level concepts, such as cats, only from watching unlabeled images taken from [YouTube](/wiki/YouTube "YouTube") videos.[[120]](#cite_note-ng2012-120)

In October 2012, [AlexNet](/wiki/AlexNet "AlexNet") by [Alex Krizhevsky](/wiki/Alex_Krizhevsky "Alex Krizhevsky"), [Ilya Sutskever](/wiki/Ilya_Sutskever "Ilya Sutskever"), and [Geoffrey Hinton](/wiki/Geoffrey_Hinton "Geoffrey Hinton")[[4]](#cite_note-krizhevsky2012-4) won the large-scale [ImageNet competition](/wiki/ImageNet_competition "ImageNet competition") by a significant margin over shallow machine learning methods. Further incremental improvements included the [VGG-16](/wiki/VGG-19 "VGG-19") network by [Karen Simonyan](/w/index.php?title=Karen_Simonyan_(scientist)&action=edit&redlink=1 "Karen Simonyan (scientist) (page does not exist)") and [Andrew Zisserman](/wiki/Andrew_Zisserman "Andrew Zisserman")[[121]](#cite_note-VGG-121) and Google's [Inceptionv3](/wiki/Inceptionv3 "Inceptionv3").[[122]](#cite_note-szegedy-122)

The success in image classification was then extended to the more challenging task of [generating descriptions](/wiki/Automatic_image_annotation "Automatic image annotation") (captions) for images, often as a combination of CNNs and LSTMs.[[123]](#cite_note-1411.4555-123)[[124]](#cite_note-1411.4952-124)[[125]](#cite_note-1411.2539-125)

In 2014, the state of the art was training “very deep neural network” with 20 to 30 layers.[[126]](#cite_note-126) Stacking too many layers led to a steep reduction in [training](/wiki/Training,_validation,_and_test_data_sets "Training, validation, and test data sets") accuracy,[[127]](#cite_note-prelu-127) known as the "degradation" problem.[[128]](#cite_note-resnet-128) In 2015, two techniques were developed to train very deep networks: the Highway Network was published in May 2015, and the [residual neural network](/wiki/Residual_neural_network "Residual neural network") (ResNet)[[129]](#cite_note-resnet20152-129) in Dec 2015. ResNet behaves like an open-gated Highway Net.

Around the same time, deep learning started impacting the field of art. Early examples included [Google DeepDream](/wiki/DeepDream "DeepDream") (2015), and [neural style transfer](/wiki/Neural_style_transfer "Neural style transfer") (2015),[[130]](#cite_note-130) both of which were based on pretrained image classification neural networks, such as [VGG-19](/wiki/VGG-19 "VGG-19").

[Generative adversarial network](/wiki/Generative_adversarial_network "Generative adversarial network") (GAN) by ([Ian Goodfellow](/wiki/Ian_Goodfellow "Ian Goodfellow") et al., 2014)[[131]](#cite_note-GANnips-131) (based on [Jürgen Schmidhuber](/wiki/J%C3%BCrgen_Schmidhuber "Jürgen Schmidhuber")'s principle of artificial curiosity[[74]](#cite_note-curiosity1991-74)[[76]](#cite_note-gancurpm2020-76)) became state of the art in generative modeling during 2014-2018 period. Excellent image quality is achieved by [Nvidia](/wiki/Nvidia "Nvidia")'s [StyleGAN](/wiki/StyleGAN "StyleGAN") (2018)[[132]](#cite_note-SyncedReview2018-132) based on the Progressive GAN by Tero Karras et al.[[133]](#cite_note-progressiveGAN2017-133) Here the GAN generator is grown from small to large scale in a pyramidal fashion. Image generation by GAN reached popular success, and provoked discussions concerning [deepfakes](/wiki/Deepfake "Deepfake").[[134]](#cite_note-134) [Diffusion models](/wiki/Diffusion_model "Diffusion model") (2015)[[135]](#cite_note-135) eclipsed GANs in generative modeling since then, with systems such as [DALL·E 2](/wiki/DALL-E "DALL-E") (2022) and [Stable Diffusion](/wiki/Stable_Diffusion "Stable Diffusion") (2022).

In 2015, Google's speech recognition improved by 49% by an LSTM-based model, which they made available through [Google Voice Search](/wiki/Google_Voice_Search "Google Voice Search") on [smartphone](/wiki/Smartphone "Smartphone").[[136]](#cite_note-GoogleVoiceTranscription-136)[[137]](#cite_note-sak2015-137)

Deep learning is part of state-of-the-art systems in various disciplines, particularly computer vision and [automatic speech recognition](/wiki/Automatic_speech_recognition "Automatic speech recognition") (ASR). Results on commonly used evaluation sets such as [TIMIT](/wiki/TIMIT "TIMIT") (ASR) and [MNIST](/wiki/MNIST_database "MNIST database") ([image classification](/wiki/Image_classification "Image classification")), as well as a range of large-vocabulary speech recognition tasks have steadily improved.[[104]](#cite_note-HintonDengYu2012-104)[[138]](#cite_note-138) Convolutional neural networks were superseded for ASR by [LSTM](/wiki/LSTM "LSTM").[[137]](#cite_note-sak2015-137)[[139]](#cite_note-sak2014-139)[[140]](#cite_note-liwu2015-140)[[141]](#cite_note-zen2015-141) but are more successful in computer vision.

[Yoshua Bengio](/wiki/Yoshua_Bengio "Yoshua Bengio"), [Geoffrey Hinton](/wiki/Geoffrey_Hinton "Geoffrey Hinton") and [Yann LeCun](/wiki/Yann_LeCun "Yann LeCun") were awarded the 2018 [Turing Award](/wiki/Turing_Award "Turing Award") for "conceptual and engineering breakthroughs that have made deep neural networks a critical component of computing".[[142]](#cite_note-142)

## Neural networks

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Deep_learning&action=edit&section=8 "Edit section: Neural networks")]

Main article: [Artificial neural network](/wiki/Artificial_neural_network "Artificial neural network")

Simplified example of training a neural network in object detection: The network is trained by multiple images that are known to depict [starfish](/wiki/Starfish "Starfish") and [sea urchins](/wiki/Sea_urchin "Sea urchin"), which are correlated with "nodes" that represent visual [features](/wiki/Feature_(computer_vision) "Feature (computer vision)"). The starfish match with a ringed texture and a star outline, whereas most sea urchins match with a striped texture and oval shape. However, the instance of a ring textured sea urchin creates a weakly weighted association between them.

Subsequent run of the network on an input image (left):[[143]](#cite_note-143) The network correctly detects the starfish. However, the weakly weighted association between ringed texture and sea urchin also confers a weak signal to the latter from one of two intermediate nodes. In addition, a [shell](/wiki/Seashell "Seashell") that was not included in the training gives a weak signal for the oval shape, also resulting in a weak signal for the sea urchin output. These weak signals may result in a [false positive](/wiki/False_positive "False positive") result for sea urchin.In reality, textures and outlines would not be represented by single nodes, but rather by associated weight patterns of multiple nodes.

**Artificial neural networks** (**ANNs**) or **[connectionist](/wiki/Connectionism "Connectionism") systems** are computing systems inspired by the [biological neural networks](/wiki/Biological_neural_network "Biological neural network") that constitute animal brains. Such systems learn (progressively improve their ability) to do tasks by considering examples, generally without task-specific programming. For example, in image recognition, they might learn to identify images that contain cats by analyzing example images that have been manually [labeled](/wiki/Labeled_data "Labeled data") as "cat" or "no cat" and using the analytic results to identify cats in other images. They have found most use in applications difficult to express with a traditional computer algorithm using [rule-based programming](/wiki/Rule-based_programming "Rule-based programming").

An ANN is based on a collection of connected units called [artificial neurons](/wiki/Artificial_neuron "Artificial neuron"), (analogous to biological [neurons](/wiki/Neuron "Neuron") in a [biological brain](/wiki/Brain "Brain")). Each connection ([synapse](/wiki/Synapse "Synapse")) between neurons can transmit a signal to another neuron. The receiving (postsynaptic) neuron can process the signal(s) and then signal downstream neurons connected to it. Neurons may have state, generally represented by [real numbers](/wiki/Real_numbers "Real numbers"), typically between 0 and 1. Neurons and synapses may also have a weight that varies as learning proceeds, which can increase or decrease the strength of the signal that it sends downstream.

Typically, neurons are organized in layers. Different layers may perform different kinds of transformations on their inputs. Signals travel from the first (input), to the last (output) layer, possibly after traversing the layers multiple times.

The original goal of the neural network approach was to solve problems in the same way that a human brain would. Over time, attention focused on matching specific mental abilities, leading to deviations from biology such as [backpropagation](/wiki/Backpropagation "Backpropagation"), or passing information in the reverse direction and adjusting the network to reflect that information.

Neural networks have been used on a variety of tasks, including computer vision, [speech recognition](/wiki/Speech_recognition "Speech recognition"), [machine translation](/wiki/Machine_translation "Machine translation"), [social network](/wiki/Social_network "Social network") filtering, [playing board and video games](/wiki/General_game_playing "General game playing") and medical diagnosis.

As of 2017, neural networks typically have a few thousand to a few million units and millions of connections. Despite this number being several order of magnitude less than the number of neurons on a human brain, these networks can perform many tasks at a level beyond that of humans (e.g., recognizing faces, or playing "Go"[[144]](#cite_note-144)).

### Deep neural networks

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Deep_learning&action=edit&section=9 "Edit section: Deep neural networks")]

A deep neural network (DNN) is an artificial neural network with multiple layers between the input and output layers.[[7]](#cite_note-BENGIODEEP-7)[[9]](#cite_note-SCHIDHUB-9) There are different types of neural networks but they always consist of the same components: neurons, synapses, weights, biases, and functions.[[145]](#cite_note-Nokkada-145) These components as a whole function in a way that mimics functions of the human brain, and can be trained like any other ML algorithm.[*[citation needed](/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation_needed "Wikipedia:Citation needed")*]

For example, a DNN that is trained to recognize dog breeds will go over the given image and calculate the probability that the dog in the image is a certain breed. The user can review the results and select which probabilities the network should display (above a certain threshold, etc.) and return the proposed label. Each mathematical manipulation as such is considered a layer,[[146]](#cite_note-Kumar2021-146) and complex DNN have many layers, hence the name "deep" networks.

DNNs can model complex non-linear relationships. DNN architectures generate compositional models where the object is expressed as a layered composition of [primitives](/wiki/Primitive_data_type "Primitive data type").[[147]](#cite_note-147) The extra layers enable composition of features from lower layers, potentially modeling complex data with fewer units than a similarly performing shallow network.[[7]](#cite_note-BENGIODEEP-7) For instance, it was proved that sparse [multivariate polynomials](/wiki/Multivariate_polynomial "Multivariate polynomial") are exponentially easier to approximate with DNNs than with shallow networks.[[148]](#cite_note-rolnickpaper-148)

Deep architectures include many variants of a few basic approaches. Each architecture has found success in specific domains. It is not always possible to compare the performance of multiple architectures, unless they have been evaluated on the same data sets.[[146]](#cite_note-Kumar2021-146)

DNNs are typically feedforward networks in which data flows from the input layer to the output layer without looping back. At first, the DNN creates a map of virtual neurons and assigns random numerical values, or "weights", to connections between them. The weights and inputs are multiplied and return an output between 0 and 1. If the network did not accurately recognize a particular pattern, an algorithm would adjust the weights.[[149]](#cite_note-149) That way the algorithm can make certain parameters more influential, until it determines the correct mathematical manipulation to fully process the data.

[Recurrent neural networks](/wiki/Recurrent_neural_networks "Recurrent neural networks"), in which data can flow in any direction, are used for applications such as [language modeling](/wiki/Language_model "Language model").[[150]](#cite_note-gers2001-150)[[151]](#cite_note-NIPS2014-151)[[152]](#cite_note-vinyals2016-152)[[153]](#cite_note-gillick2015-153)[[154]](#cite_note-MIKO2010-154) Long short-term memory is particularly effective for this use.[[155]](#cite_note-:0-155)[[156]](#cite_note-:10-156)

[Convolutional neural networks](/wiki/Convolutional_neural_network "Convolutional neural network") (CNNs) are used in computer vision.[[157]](#cite_note-LECUN86-157) CNNs also have been applied to [acoustic modeling](/wiki/Acoustic_model "Acoustic model") for automatic speech recognition (ASR).[[158]](#cite_note-:2-158)

#### Challenges

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Deep_learning&action=edit&section=10 "Edit section: Challenges")]

As with ANNs, many issues can arise with naively trained DNNs. Two common issues are [overfitting](/wiki/Overfitting "Overfitting") and computation time.

DNNs are prone to overfitting because of the added layers of abstraction, which allow them to model rare dependencies in the training data. [Regularization](/wiki/Regularization_(mathematics) "Regularization (mathematics)") methods such as Ivakhnenko's unit pruning[[41]](#cite_note-ivak1971-41) or [weight decay](/wiki/Weight_decay "Weight decay") (-regularization) or [sparsity](/wiki/Sparse_matrix "Sparse matrix") (-regularization) can be applied during training to combat overfitting.[[159]](#cite_note-159) Alternatively [dropout](/wiki/Dropout_(neural_networks) "Dropout (neural networks)") regularization randomly omits units from the hidden layers during training. This helps to exclude rare dependencies.[[160]](#cite_note-DAHL2013-160) Another interesting recent development is research into models of just enough complexity through an estimation of the intrinsic complexity of the task being modelled. This approach has been successfully applied for multivariate time series prediction tasks such as traffic prediction.[[161]](#cite_note-Kumar2024-161) Finally, data can be augmented via methods such as cropping and rotating such that smaller training sets can be increased in size to reduce the chances of overfitting.[[162]](#cite_note-162)

DNNs must consider many training parameters, such as the size (number of layers and number of units per layer), the [learning rate](/wiki/Learning_rate "Learning rate"), and initial weights. [Sweeping through the parameter space](/wiki/Hyperparameter_optimization#Grid_search "Hyperparameter optimization") for optimal parameters may not be feasible due to the cost in time and computational resources. Various tricks, such as [batching](/wiki/Batch_learning "Batch learning") (computing the gradient on several training examples at once rather than individual examples)[[163]](#cite_note-RBMTRAIN-163) speed up computation. Large processing capabilities of many-core architectures (such as GPUs or the Intel Xeon Phi) have produced significant speedups in training, because of the suitability of such processing architectures for the matrix and vector computations.[[164]](#cite_note-164)[[165]](#cite_note-165)

Alternatively, engineers may look for other types of neural networks with more straightforward and convergent training algorithms. CMAC ([cerebellar model articulation controller](/wiki/Cerebellar_model_articulation_controller "Cerebellar model articulation controller")) is one such kind of neural network. It doesn't require learning rates or randomized initial weights. The training process can be guaranteed to converge in one step with a new batch of data, and the computational complexity of the training algorithm is linear with respect to the number of neurons involved.[[166]](#cite_note-Qin1-166)[[167]](#cite_note-Qin2-167)

## Hardware

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Deep_learning&action=edit&section=11 "Edit section: Hardware")]

Since the 2010s, advances in both machine learning algorithms and [computer hardware](/wiki/Computer_hardware "Computer hardware") have led to more efficient methods for training deep neural networks that contain many layers of non-linear hidden units and a very large output layer.[[168]](#cite_note-168) By 2019, [graphics processing units](/wiki/Graphics_processing_unit "Graphics processing unit") (GPUs), often with AI-specific enhancements, had displaced CPUs as the dominant method for training large-scale commercial cloud AI .[[169]](#cite_note-169) [OpenAI](/wiki/OpenAI "OpenAI") estimated the hardware computation used in the largest deep learning projects from AlexNet (2012) to AlphaZero (2017) and found a 300,000-fold increase in the amount of computation required, with a doubling-time trendline of 3.4 months.[[170]](#cite_note-170)[[171]](#cite_note-171)

Special [electronic circuits](/wiki/Electronic_circuit "Electronic circuit") called [deep learning processors](/wiki/Deep_learning_processor "Deep learning processor") were designed to speed up deep learning algorithms. Deep learning processors include neural processing units (NPUs) in [Huawei](/wiki/Huawei "Huawei") cellphones[[172]](#cite_note-172) and [cloud computing](/wiki/Cloud_computing "Cloud computing") servers such as [tensor processing units](/wiki/Tensor_processing_unit "Tensor processing unit") (TPU) in the [Google Cloud Platform](/wiki/Google_Cloud_Platform "Google Cloud Platform").[[173]](#cite_note-173) [Cerebras Systems](/wiki/Cerebras "Cerebras") has also built a dedicated system to handle large deep learning models, the CS-2, based on the largest processor in the industry, the second-generation Wafer Scale Engine (WSE-2).[[174]](#cite_note-174)[[175]](#cite_note-175)

Atomically thin [semiconductors](/wiki/Semiconductors "Semiconductors") are considered promising for energy-efficient deep learning hardware where the same basic device structure is used for both logic operations and data storage. In 2020, Marega et al. published experiments with a large-area active channel material for developing logic-in-memory devices and circuits based on [floating-gate](/wiki/Floating-gate "Floating-gate") [field-effect transistors](/wiki/Field-effect_transistor "Field-effect transistor") (FGFETs).[[176]](#cite_note-atomthin-176)

In 2021, J. Feldmann et al. proposed an integrated [photonic](/wiki/Photonic "Photonic") [hardware accelerator](/wiki/Hardware_accelerator "Hardware accelerator") for parallel convolutional processing.[[177]](#cite_note-photonic-177) The authors identify two key advantages of integrated photonics over its electronic counterparts: (1) massively parallel data transfer through [wavelength](/wiki/Wavelength "Wavelength") division [multiplexing](/wiki/Multiplexing "Multiplexing") in conjunction with [frequency combs](/wiki/Frequency_comb "Frequency comb"), and (2) extremely high data modulation speeds.[[177]](#cite_note-photonic-177) Their system can execute trillions of multiply-accumulate operations per second, indicating the potential of [integrated](/wiki/Photonic_integrated_circuit "Photonic integrated circuit") [photonics](/wiki/Photonics "Photonics") in data-heavy AI applications.[[177]](#cite_note-photonic-177)

## Applications

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Deep_learning&action=edit&section=12 "Edit section: Applications")]

### Automatic speech recognition

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Deep_learning&action=edit&section=13 "Edit section: Automatic speech recognition")]

Main article: [Speech recognition](/wiki/Speech_recognition "Speech recognition")

Large-scale automatic speech recognition is the first and most convincing successful case of deep learning. LSTM RNNs can learn "Very Deep Learning" tasks[[9]](#cite_note-SCHIDHUB-9) that involve multi-second intervals containing speech events separated by thousands of discrete time steps, where one time step corresponds to about 10 ms. LSTM with forget gates[[156]](#cite_note-:10-156) is competitive with traditional speech recognizers on certain tasks.[[93]](#cite_note-graves2003-93)

The initial success in speech recognition was based on small-scale recognition tasks based on TIMIT. The data set contains 630 speakers from eight major [dialects](/wiki/Dialect "Dialect") of [American English](/wiki/American_English "American English"), where each speaker reads 10 sentences.[[178]](#cite_note-APC_1-178) Its small size lets many configurations be tried. More importantly, the TIMIT task concerns [phone](/wiki/Phone_(phonetics) "Phone (phonetics)")-sequence recognition, which, unlike word-sequence recognition, allows weak phone [bigram](/wiki/Bigram "Bigram") language models. This lets the strength of the acoustic modeling aspects of speech recognition be more easily analyzed. The error rates listed below, including these early results and measured as percent phone error rates (PER), have been summarized since 1991.

| Method | Percent phoneerror rate (PER) (%) |
| --- | --- |
| Randomly Initialized RNN[[179]](#cite_note-179) | 26.1 |
| Bayesian Triphone GMM-HMM | 25.6 |
| Hidden Trajectory (Generative) Model | 24.8 |
| Monophone Randomly Initialized DNN | 23.4 |
| Monophone DBN-DNN | 22.4 |
| Triphone GMM-HMM with BMMI Training | 21.7 |
| Monophone DBN-DNN on fbank | 20.7 |
| Convolutional DNN[[180]](#cite_note-CNN-2014-180) | 20.0 |
| Convolutional DNN w. Heterogeneous Pooling | 18.7 |
| Ensemble DNN/CNN/RNN[[181]](#cite_note-EnsembleDL-181) | 18.3 |
| Bidirectional LSTM | 17.8 |
| Hierarchical Convolutional Deep Maxout Network[[182]](#cite_note-HCDMM-182) | 16.5 |

The debut of DNNs for speaker recognition in the late 1990s and speech recognition around 2009-2011 and of LSTM around 2003–2007, accelerated progress in eight major areas:[[23]](#cite_note-BOOK2014-23)[[108]](#cite_note-interspeech2014Keynote-108)[[106]](#cite_note-ReferenceA-106)

* Scale-up/out and accelerated DNN training and decoding
* Sequence discriminative training
* Feature processing by deep models with solid understanding of the underlying mechanisms
* Adaptation of DNNs and related deep models
* [Multi-task](/wiki/Multi-task_learning "Multi-task learning") and [transfer learning](/wiki/Transfer_learning "Transfer learning") by DNNs and related deep models
* [CNNs](/wiki/Convolutional_neural_network "Convolutional neural network") and how to design them to best exploit [domain knowledge](/wiki/Domain_knowledge "Domain knowledge") of speech
* [RNN](/wiki/Recurrent_neural_network "Recurrent neural network") and its rich LSTM variants
* Other types of deep models including tensor-based models and integrated deep generative/discriminative models.

More recent speech recognition models use [Transformers](/wiki/Transformer_(deep_learning_architecture) "Transformer (deep learning architecture)") or [Temporal Convolution Networks](/wiki/Time_delay_neural_network "Time delay neural network") with significant success and widespread applications.[[183]](#cite_note-183)[[184]](#cite_note-184)[[185]](#cite_note-185) All major commercial speech recognition systems (e.g., Microsoft [Cortana](/wiki/Cortana_(software) "Cortana (software)"), [Xbox](/wiki/Xbox "Xbox"), [Skype Translator](/wiki/Skype_Translator "Skype Translator"), [Amazon Alexa](/wiki/Amazon_Alexa "Amazon Alexa"), [Google Now](/wiki/Google_Now "Google Now"), [Apple Siri](/wiki/Siri "Siri"), [Baidu](/wiki/Baidu "Baidu") and [iFlyTek](/wiki/IFlytek "IFlytek") voice search, and a range of [Nuance](/wiki/Nuance_Communications "Nuance Communications") speech products, etc.) are based on deep learning.[[23]](#cite_note-BOOK2014-23)[[186]](#cite_note-186)[[187]](#cite_note-Baidu-187)

### Image recognition

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Deep_learning&action=edit&section=14 "Edit section: Image recognition")]

Main article: [Computer vision](/wiki/Computer_vision "Computer vision")

A common evaluation set for image classification is the [MNIST database](/wiki/MNIST_database "MNIST database") data set. MNIST is composed of handwritten digits and includes 60,000 training examples and 10,000 test examples. As with TIMIT, its small size lets users test multiple configurations. A comprehensive list of results on this set is available.[[188]](#cite_note-YANNMNIST-188)

Deep learning-based image recognition has become "superhuman", producing more accurate results than human contestants. This first occurred in 2011 in recognition of traffic signs, and in 2014, with recognition of human faces.[[189]](#cite_note-:7-189)[[190]](#cite_note-surpass1-190)

Deep learning-trained vehicles now interpret 360° camera views.[[191]](#cite_note-191) Another example is Facial Dysmorphology Novel Analysis (FDNA) used to analyze cases of human malformation connected to a large database of genetic syndromes.

### Visual art processing

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Deep_learning&action=edit&section=15 "Edit section: Visual art processing")]

Closely related to the progress that has been made in image recognition is the increasing application of deep learning techniques to various visual art tasks. DNNs have proven themselves capable, for example, of

* identifying the style period of a given painting[[192]](#cite_note-art1-192)[[193]](#cite_note-art2-193)
* [Neural Style Transfer](/wiki/Neural_Style_Transfer "Neural Style Transfer") – capturing the style of a given artwork and applying it in a visually pleasing manner to an arbitrary photograph or video[[192]](#cite_note-art1-192)[[193]](#cite_note-art2-193)
* generating striking imagery based on random visual input fields.[[192]](#cite_note-art1-192)[[193]](#cite_note-art2-193)

### Natural language processing

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Deep_learning&action=edit&section=16 "Edit section: Natural language processing")]

Main article: [Natural language processing](/wiki/Natural_language_processing "Natural language processing")

Neural networks have been used for implementing language models since the early 2000s.[[150]](#cite_note-gers2001-150) LSTM helped to improve machine translation and language modeling.[[151]](#cite_note-NIPS2014-151)[[152]](#cite_note-vinyals2016-152)[[153]](#cite_note-gillick2015-153)

Other key techniques in this field are negative sampling[[194]](#cite_note-GoldbergLevy2014-194) and [word embedding](/wiki/Word_embedding "Word embedding"). Word embedding, such as *[word2vec](/wiki/Word2vec "Word2vec")*, can be thought of as a representational layer in a deep learning architecture that transforms an atomic word into a positional representation of the word relative to other words in the dataset; the position is represented as a point in a [vector space](/wiki/Vector_space "Vector space"). Using word embedding as an RNN input layer allows the network to parse sentences and phrases using an effective compositional vector grammar. A compositional vector grammar can be thought of as [probabilistic context free grammar](/wiki/Probabilistic_context_free_grammar "Probabilistic context free grammar") (PCFG) implemented by an RNN.[[195]](#cite_note-SocherManning2014-195) Recursive auto-encoders built atop word embeddings can assess sentence similarity and detect paraphrasing.[[195]](#cite_note-SocherManning2014-195) Deep neural architectures provide the best results for constituency parsing,[[196]](#cite_note-196) [sentiment analysis](/wiki/Sentiment_analysis "Sentiment analysis"),[[197]](#cite_note-RDM_1-197) information retrieval,[[198]](#cite_note-198)[[199]](#cite_note-199) spoken language understanding,[[200]](#cite_note-IEEE-TASL2015-200) machine translation,[[151]](#cite_note-NIPS2014-151)[[201]](#cite_note-auto-201) contextual entity linking,[[201]](#cite_note-auto-201) writing style recognition,[[202]](#cite_note-BROC2017-202) [named-entity recognition](/wiki/Named-entity_recognition "Named-entity recognition") (token classification),[[203]](#cite_note-203) text classification, and others.[[204]](#cite_note-204)

Recent developments generalize [word embedding](/wiki/Word_embedding "Word embedding") to [sentence embedding](/wiki/Sentence_embedding "Sentence embedding").

[Google Translate](/wiki/Google_Translate "Google Translate") (GT) uses a large end-to-end [long short-term memory](/wiki/Long_short-term_memory "Long short-term memory") (LSTM) network.[[205]](#cite_note-GT_Turovsky_2016-205)[[206]](#cite_note-googleblog_GNMT_2016-206)[[207]](#cite_note-GoogleTranslate-207)[[208]](#cite_note-WiredGoogleTranslate-208) [Google Neural Machine Translation (GNMT)](/wiki/Google_Neural_Machine_Translation "Google Neural Machine Translation") uses an [example-based machine translation](/wiki/Example-based_machine_translation "Example-based machine translation") method in which the system "learns from millions of examples".[[206]](#cite_note-googleblog_GNMT_2016-206) It translates "whole sentences at a time, rather than pieces". Google Translate supports over one hundred languages.[[206]](#cite_note-googleblog_GNMT_2016-206) The network encodes the "semantics of the sentence rather than simply memorizing phrase-to-phrase translations".[[206]](#cite_note-googleblog_GNMT_2016-206)[[209]](#cite_note-Biotet-209) GT uses English as an intermediate between most language pairs.[[209]](#cite_note-Biotet-209)

### Drug discovery and toxicology

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Deep_learning&action=edit&section=17 "Edit section: Drug discovery and toxicology")]

For more information, see [Drug discovery](/wiki/Drug_discovery "Drug discovery") and [Toxicology](/wiki/Toxicology "Toxicology").

A large percentage of candidate drugs fail to win regulatory approval. These failures are caused by insufficient efficacy (on-target effect), undesired interactions (off-target effects), or unanticipated [toxic effects](/wiki/Toxicity "Toxicity").[[210]](#cite_note-ARROWSMITH2013-210)[[211]](#cite_note-VERBIEST2015-211) Research has explored use of deep learning to predict the [biomolecular targets](/wiki/Biomolecular_target "Biomolecular target"),[[212]](#cite_note-MERCK2012-212)[[213]](#cite_note-:5-213) [off-targets](/wiki/Off-target "Off-target"), and [toxic effects](/wiki/Toxicity "Toxicity") of environmental chemicals in nutrients, household products and drugs.[[214]](#cite_note-TOX21-214)[[215]](#cite_note-TOX21Data-215)[[216]](#cite_note-:11-216)

AtomNet is a deep learning system for structure-based [rational drug design](/wiki/Drug_design "Drug design").[[217]](#cite_note-217) AtomNet was used to predict novel candidate biomolecules for disease targets such as the [Ebola virus](/wiki/Ebola_virus "Ebola virus")[[218]](#cite_note-Toronto-218) and [multiple sclerosis](/wiki/Multiple_sclerosis "Multiple sclerosis").[[219]](#cite_note-219)[[218]](#cite_note-Toronto-218)

In 2017 [graph neural networks](/wiki/Graph_neural_network "Graph neural network") were used for the first time to predict various properties of molecules in a large toxicology data set.[[220]](#cite_note-220) In 2019, generative neural networks were used to produce molecules that were validated experimentally all the way into mice.[[221]](#cite_note-221)[[222]](#cite_note-222)

### Customer relationship management

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Deep_learning&action=edit&section=18 "Edit section: Customer relationship management")]

Main article: [Customer relationship management](/wiki/Customer_relationship_management "Customer relationship management")

[Deep reinforcement learning](/wiki/Deep_reinforcement_learning "Deep reinforcement learning") has been used to approximate the value of possible [direct marketing](/wiki/Direct_marketing "Direct marketing") actions, defined in terms of [RFM](/wiki/RFM_(customer_value) "RFM (customer value)") variables. The estimated value function was shown to have a natural interpretation as [customer lifetime value](/wiki/Customer_lifetime_value "Customer lifetime value").[[223]](#cite_note-223)

### Recommendation systems

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Deep_learning&action=edit&section=19 "Edit section: Recommendation systems")]

Main article: [Recommender system](/wiki/Recommender_system "Recommender system")

Recommendation systems have used deep learning to extract meaningful features for a latent factor model for content-based music and journal recommendations.[[224]](#cite_note-224)[[225]](#cite_note-225) Multi-view deep learning has been applied for learning user preferences from multiple domains.[[226]](#cite_note-226) The model uses a hybrid collaborative and content-based approach and enhances recommendations in multiple tasks.

### Bioinformatics

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Deep_learning&action=edit&section=20 "Edit section: Bioinformatics")]

Main article: [Bioinformatics](/wiki/Bioinformatics "Bioinformatics")

An [autoencoder](/wiki/Autoencoder "Autoencoder") ANN was used in [bioinformatics](/wiki/Bioinformatics "Bioinformatics"), to predict [gene ontology](/wiki/Gene_Ontology "Gene Ontology") annotations and gene-function relationships.[[227]](#cite_note-227)

In medical informatics, deep learning was used to predict sleep quality based on data from wearables[[228]](#cite_note-228) and predictions of health complications from [electronic health record](/wiki/Electronic_health_record "Electronic health record") data.[[229]](#cite_note-229)

Deep neural networks have shown unparalleled performance in [predicting protein structure](/wiki/Protein_structure_prediction "Protein structure prediction"), according to the sequence of the amino acids that make it up. In 2020, [AlphaFold](/wiki/AlphaFold "AlphaFold"), a deep-learning based system, achieved a level of accuracy significantly higher than all previous computational methods.[[230]](#cite_note-230)[[231]](#cite_note-231)

### Deep Neural Network Estimations

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Deep_learning&action=edit&section=21 "Edit section: Deep Neural Network Estimations")]

Deep neural networks can be used to estimate the entropy of a [stochastic process](/wiki/Stochastic_process "Stochastic process") and called Neural Joint Entropy Estimator (NJEE).[[232]](#cite_note-SPB22-232) Such an estimation provides insights on the effects of input [random variables](/wiki/Random_variables "Random variables") on an independent [random variable](/wiki/Random_variable "Random variable"). Practically, the DNN is trained as a [classifier](/wiki/Classifier_(machine_learning) "Classifier (machine learning)") that maps an input [vector](/wiki/Vector_(mathematics_and_physics) "Vector (mathematics and physics)") or [matrix](/wiki/Matrix_(mathematics) "Matrix (mathematics)") X to an output [probability distribution](/wiki/Probability_distribution "Probability distribution") over the possible classes of random variable Y, given input X. For example, in [image classification](/wiki/Image_classification "Image classification") tasks, the NJEE maps a vector of [pixels](/wiki/Pixels "Pixels")' color values to probabilities over possible image classes. In practice, the probability distribution of Y is obtained by a [Softmax](/wiki/Softmax "Softmax") layer with number of nodes that is equal to the [alphabet](/wiki/Alphabet "Alphabet") size of Y. NJEE uses continuously differentiable [activation functions](/wiki/Activation_function "Activation function"), such that the conditions for the [universal approximation theorem](/wiki/Universal_approximation_theorem "Universal approximation theorem") holds. It is shown that this method provides a strongly [consistent estimator](/wiki/Consistent_estimator "Consistent estimator") and outperforms other methods in case of large alphabet sizes.[[232]](#cite_note-SPB22-232)

### Medical image analysis

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Deep_learning&action=edit&section=22 "Edit section: Medical image analysis")]

Deep learning has been shown to produce competitive results in medical application such as cancer cell classification, lesion detection, organ segmentation and image enhancement.[[233]](#cite_note-233)[[234]](#cite_note-234) Modern deep learning tools demonstrate the high accuracy of detecting various diseases and the helpfulness of their use by specialists to improve the diagnosis efficiency.[[235]](#cite_note-235)[[236]](#cite_note-236)

### Mobile advertising

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Deep_learning&action=edit&section=23 "Edit section: Mobile advertising")]

Finding the appropriate mobile audience for [mobile advertising](/wiki/Mobile_advertising "Mobile advertising") is always challenging, since many data points must be considered and analyzed before a target segment can be created and used in ad serving by any ad server.[[237]](#cite_note-237) Deep learning has been used to interpret large, many-dimensioned advertising datasets. Many data points are collected during the request/serve/click internet advertising cycle. This information can form the basis of machine learning to improve ad selection.

### Image restoration

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Deep_learning&action=edit&section=24 "Edit section: Image restoration")]

Deep learning has been successfully applied to [inverse problems](/wiki/Inverse_problems "Inverse problems") such as [denoising](/wiki/Denoising "Denoising"), [super-resolution](/wiki/Super-resolution "Super-resolution"), [inpainting](/wiki/Inpainting "Inpainting"), and [film colorization](/wiki/Film_colorization "Film colorization").[[238]](#cite_note-238) These applications include learning methods such as "Shrinkage Fields for Effective Image Restoration"[[239]](#cite_note-239) which trains on an image dataset, and [Deep Image Prior](/wiki/Deep_Image_Prior "Deep Image Prior"), which trains on the image that needs restoration.

### Financial fraud detection

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Deep_learning&action=edit&section=25 "Edit section: Financial fraud detection")]

Deep learning is being successfully applied to financial [fraud detection](/wiki/Fraud_detection "Fraud detection"), tax evasion detection,[[240]](#cite_note-240) and anti-money laundering.[[241]](#cite_note-241)

### Materials science

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Deep_learning&action=edit&section=26 "Edit section: Materials science")]

In November 2023, researchers at [Google DeepMind](/wiki/Google_DeepMind "Google DeepMind") and [Lawrence Berkeley National Laboratory](/wiki/Lawrence_Berkeley_National_Laboratory "Lawrence Berkeley National Laboratory") announced that they had developed an AI system known as GNoME. This system has contributed to [materials science](/wiki/Materials_science "Materials science") by discovering over 2 million new materials within a relatively short timeframe. GNoME employs deep learning techniques to efficiently explore potential material structures, achieving a significant increase in the identification of stable inorganic [crystal structures](/wiki/Crystal_structure "Crystal structure"). The system's predictions were validated through autonomous robotic experiments, demonstrating a noteworthy success rate of 71%. The data of newly discovered materials is publicly available through the [Materials Project](/wiki/Materials_Project "Materials Project") database, offering researchers the opportunity to identify materials with desired properties for various applications. This development has implications for the future of scientific discovery and the integration of AI in material science research, potentially expediting material innovation and reducing costs in product development. The use of AI and deep learning suggests the possibility of minimizing or eliminating manual lab experiments and allowing scientists to focus more on the design and analysis of unique compounds.[[242]](#cite_note-242)[[243]](#cite_note-243)[[244]](#cite_note-244)

### Military

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Deep_learning&action=edit&section=27 "Edit section: Military")]

The United States Department of Defense applied deep learning to train robots in new tasks through observation.[[245]](#cite_note-:12-245)

### Partial differential equations

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Deep_learning&action=edit&section=28 "Edit section: Partial differential equations")]

Physics informed neural networks have been used to solve [partial differential equations](/wiki/Partial_differential_equation "Partial differential equation") in both forward and inverse problems in a data driven manner.[[246]](#cite_note-246) One example is the reconstructing fluid flow governed by the [Navier-Stokes equations](/wiki/Navier%E2%80%93Stokes_equations "Navier–Stokes equations"). Using physics informed neural networks does not require the often expensive mesh generation that conventional [CFD](/wiki/Computational_fluid_dynamics "Computational fluid dynamics") methods rely on.[[247]](#cite_note-247)[[248]](#cite_note-248)

### Deep backward stochastic differential equation method

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Deep_learning&action=edit&section=29 "Edit section: Deep backward stochastic differential equation method")]

[Deep backward stochastic differential equation method](/wiki/Deep_backward_stochastic_differential_equation_method "Deep backward stochastic differential equation method") is a numerical method that combines deep learning with [Backward stochastic differential equation](/wiki/Backward_stochastic_differential_equation "Backward stochastic differential equation") (BSDE). This method is particularly useful for solving high-dimensional problems in financial mathematics. By leveraging the powerful function approximation capabilities of [deep neural networks](/wiki/Deep_neural_networks "Deep neural networks"), deep BSDE addresses the computational challenges faced by traditional numerical methods in high-dimensional settings. Specifically, traditional methods like finite difference methods or Monte Carlo simulations often struggle with the curse of dimensionality, where computational cost increases exponentially with the number of dimensions. Deep BSDE methods, however, employ deep neural networks to approximate solutions of high-dimensional partial differential equations (PDEs), effectively reducing the computational burden.[[249]](#cite_note-Han2018-249)

In addition, the integration of [Physics-informed neural networks](/wiki/Physics-informed_neural_networks "Physics-informed neural networks") (PINNs) into the deep BSDE framework enhances its capability by embedding the underlying physical laws directly into the neural network architecture. This ensures that the solutions not only fit the data but also adhere to the governing stochastic differential equations. PINNs leverage the power of deep learning while respecting the constraints imposed by the physical models, resulting in more accurate and reliable solutions for financial mathematics problems.

### Image reconstruction

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Deep_learning&action=edit&section=30 "Edit section: Image reconstruction")]

Image reconstruction is the reconstruction of the underlying images from the image-related measurements. Several works showed the better and superior performance of the deep learning methods compared to analytical methods for various applications, e.g., spectral imaging [[250]](#cite_note-250) and ultrasound imaging.[[251]](#cite_note-251)

### Weather prediction

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Deep_learning&action=edit&section=31 "Edit section: Weather prediction")]

Traditional weather prediction systems solve a very complex system of partial differential equations. GraphCast is a deep learning based model, trained on a long history of weather data to predict how weather patterns change over time. It is able to predict weather conditions for up to 10 days globally, at a very detailed level, and in under a minute, with precision similar to state of the art systems.[[252]](#cite_note-252)[[253]](#cite_note-253)

### Epigenetic clock

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Deep_learning&action=edit&section=32 "Edit section: Epigenetic clock")]

Main article: [Epigenetic clock](/wiki/Epigenetic_clock "Epigenetic clock")

An epigenetic clock is a [biochemical test](/wiki/Biomarkers_of_aging "Biomarkers of aging") that can be used to measure age. Galkin et al. used deep neural networks to train an epigenetic aging clock of unprecedented accuracy using >6,000 blood samples.[[254]](#cite_note-254) The clock uses information from 1000 [CpG sites](/wiki/CpG_site "CpG site") and predicts people with certain conditions older than healthy controls: [IBD](/wiki/Inflammatory_bowel_disease "Inflammatory bowel disease"), [frontotemporal dementia](/wiki/Frontotemporal_dementia "Frontotemporal dementia"), [ovarian cancer](/wiki/Ovarian_cancer "Ovarian cancer"), [obesity](/wiki/Obesity "Obesity"). The aging clock was planned to be released for public use in 2021 by an [Insilico Medicine](/wiki/Insilico_Medicine "Insilico Medicine") spinoff company Deep Longevity.

## Relation to human cognitive and brain development

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Deep_learning&action=edit&section=33 "Edit section: Relation to human cognitive and brain development")]

Deep learning is closely related to a class of theories of [brain development](/wiki/Brain_development "Brain development") (specifically, neocortical development) proposed by [cognitive neuroscientists](/wiki/Cognitive_neuroscientist "Cognitive neuroscientist") in the early 1990s.[[255]](#cite_note-UTGOFF-255)[[256]](#cite_note-ELMAN-256)[[257]](#cite_note-SHRAGER-257)[[258]](#cite_note-QUARTZ-258) These developmental theories were instantiated in computational models, making them predecessors of deep learning systems. These developmental models share the property that various proposed learning dynamics in the brain (e.g., a wave of [nerve growth factor](/wiki/Nerve_growth_factor "Nerve growth factor")) support the [self-organization](/wiki/Self-organization "Self-organization") somewhat analogous to the neural networks utilized in deep learning models. Like the [neocortex](/wiki/Neocortex "Neocortex"), neural networks employ a hierarchy of layered filters in which each layer considers information from a prior layer (or the operating environment), and then passes its output (and possibly the original input), to other layers. This process yields a self-organizing stack of [transducers](/wiki/Transducer "Transducer"), well-tuned to their operating environment. A 1995 description stated, "...the infant's brain seems to organize itself under the influence of waves of so-called trophic-factors ... different regions of the brain become connected sequentially, with one layer of tissue maturing before another and so on until the whole brain is mature".[[259]](#cite_note-BLAKESLEE-259)

A variety of approaches have been used to investigate the plausibility of deep learning models from a neurobiological perspective. On the one hand, several variants of the [backpropagation](/wiki/Backpropagation "Backpropagation") algorithm have been proposed in order to increase its processing realism.[[260]](#cite_note-260)[[261]](#cite_note-261) Other researchers have argued that unsupervised forms of deep learning, such as those based on hierarchical [generative models](/wiki/Generative_model "Generative model") and [deep belief networks](/wiki/Deep_belief_network "Deep belief network"), may be closer to biological reality.[[262]](#cite_note-262)[[263]](#cite_note-263) In this respect, generative neural network models have been related to neurobiological evidence about sampling-based processing in the cerebral cortex.[[264]](#cite_note-264)

Although a systematic comparison between the human brain organization and the neuronal encoding in deep networks has not yet been established, several analogies have been reported. For example, the computations performed by deep learning units could be similar to those of actual neurons[[265]](#cite_note-265) and neural populations.[[266]](#cite_note-266) Similarly, the representations developed by deep learning models are similar to those measured in the primate visual system[[267]](#cite_note-267) both at the single-unit[[268]](#cite_note-268) and at the population[[269]](#cite_note-269) levels.

## Commercial activity

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Deep_learning&action=edit&section=34 "Edit section: Commercial activity")]

[Facebook](/wiki/Facebook "Facebook")'s AI lab performs tasks such as [automatically tagging uploaded pictures](/wiki/Automatic_image_annotation "Automatic image annotation") with the names of the people in them.[[270]](#cite_note-METZ2013-270)

Google's [DeepMind Technologies](/wiki/DeepMind_Technologies "DeepMind Technologies") developed a system capable of learning how to play [Atari](/wiki/Atari "Atari") video games using only pixels as data input. In 2015 they demonstrated their [AlphaGo](/wiki/AlphaGo "AlphaGo") system, which learned the game of [Go](/wiki/Go_(game) "Go (game)") well enough to beat a professional Go player.[[271]](#cite_note-271)[[272]](#cite_note-272)[[273]](#cite_note-273) [Google Translate](/wiki/Google_Translate "Google Translate") uses a neural network to translate between more than 100 languages.

In 2017, Covariant.ai was launched, which focuses on integrating deep learning into factories.[[274]](#cite_note-274)

As of 2008,[[275]](#cite_note-275) researchers at [The University of Texas at Austin](/wiki/University_of_Texas_at_Austin "University of Texas at Austin") (UT) developed a machine learning framework called Training an Agent Manually via Evaluative Reinforcement, or TAMER, which proposed new methods for robots or computer programs to learn how to perform tasks by interacting with a human instructor.[[245]](#cite_note-:12-245) First developed as TAMER, a new algorithm called Deep TAMER was later introduced in 2018 during a collaboration between [U.S. Army Research Laboratory](/wiki/U.S._Army_Research_Laboratory "U.S. Army Research Laboratory") (ARL) and UT researchers. Deep TAMER used deep learning to provide a robot with the ability to learn new tasks through observation.[[245]](#cite_note-:12-245) Using Deep TAMER, a robot learned a task with a human trainer, watching video streams or observing a human perform a task in-person. The robot later practiced the task with the help of some coaching from the trainer, who provided feedback such as "good job" and "bad job".[[276]](#cite_note-276)

## Criticism and comment

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Deep_learning&action=edit&section=35 "Edit section: Criticism and comment")]

Deep learning has attracted both criticism and comment, in some cases from outside the field of computer science.

### Theory

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Deep_learning&action=edit&section=36 "Edit section: Theory")]

See also: [Explainable artificial intelligence](/wiki/Explainable_artificial_intelligence "Explainable artificial intelligence")

A main criticism concerns the lack of theory surrounding some methods.[[277]](#cite_note-277) Learning in the most common deep architectures is implemented using well-understood gradient descent. However, the theory surrounding other algorithms, such as contrastive divergence is less clear.[*[citation needed](/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation_needed "Wikipedia:Citation needed")*] (e.g., Does it converge? If so, how fast? What is it approximating?) Deep learning methods are often looked at as a [black box](/wiki/Black_box "Black box"), with most confirmations done empirically, rather than theoretically.[[278]](#cite_note-Knight_2017-278)

In further reference to the idea that artistic sensitivity might be inherent in relatively low levels of the cognitive hierarchy, a published series of graphic representations of the internal states of deep (20-30 layers) neural networks attempting to discern within essentially random data the images on which they were trained[[279]](#cite_note-279) demonstrate a visual appeal: the original research notice received well over 1,000 comments, and was the subject of what was for a time the most frequently accessed article on *[The Guardian](/wiki/The_Guardian "The Guardian")'s*[[280]](#cite_note-280) website.

### Errors

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Deep_learning&action=edit&section=37 "Edit section: Errors")]

Some deep learning architectures display problematic behaviors,[[281]](#cite_note-goertzel-281) such as confidently classifying unrecognizable images as belonging to a familiar category of ordinary images (2014)[[282]](#cite_note-282) and misclassifying minuscule perturbations of correctly classified images (2013).[[283]](#cite_note-283) [Goertzel](/wiki/Ben_Goertzel "Ben Goertzel") hypothesized that these behaviors are due to limitations in their internal representations and that these limitations would inhibit integration into heterogeneous multi-component [artificial general intelligence](/wiki/Artificial_general_intelligence "Artificial general intelligence") (AGI) architectures.[[281]](#cite_note-goertzel-281) These issues may possibly be addressed by deep learning architectures that internally form states homologous to image-grammar[[284]](#cite_note-284) decompositions of observed entities and events.[[281]](#cite_note-goertzel-281) [Learning a grammar](/wiki/Grammar_induction "Grammar induction") (visual or linguistic) from training data would be equivalent to restricting the system to [commonsense reasoning](/wiki/Commonsense_reasoning "Commonsense reasoning") that operates on concepts in terms of grammatical [production rules](/wiki/Production_(computer_science) "Production (computer science)") and is a basic goal of both human language acquisition[[285]](#cite_note-285) and [artificial intelligence](/wiki/Artificial_intelligence "Artificial intelligence") (AI).[[286]](#cite_note-286)

### Cyber threat

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Deep_learning&action=edit&section=38 "Edit section: Cyber threat")]

As deep learning moves from the lab into the world, research and experience show that artificial neural networks are vulnerable to hacks and deception.[[287]](#cite_note-287) By identifying patterns that these systems use to function, attackers can modify inputs to ANNs in such a way that the ANN finds a match that human observers would not recognize. For example, an attacker can make subtle changes to an image such that the ANN finds a match even though the image looks to a human nothing like the search target. Such manipulation is termed an "[adversarial attack](/wiki/Adversarial_machine_learning "Adversarial machine learning")".[[288]](#cite_note-288)

In 2016 researchers used one ANN to doctor images in trial and error fashion, identify another's focal points, and thereby generate images that deceived it. The modified images looked no different to human eyes. Another group showed that printouts of doctored images then photographed successfully tricked an image classification system.[[289]](#cite_note-:4-289) One defense is reverse image search, in which a possible fake image is submitted to a site such as [TinEye](/wiki/TinEye "TinEye") that can then find other instances of it. A refinement is to search using only parts of the image, to identify images from which that piece may have been taken**.**[[290]](#cite_note-290)

Another group showed that certain [psychedelic](/wiki/Psychedelic_art "Psychedelic art") spectacles could fool a [facial recognition system](/wiki/Facial_recognition_system "Facial recognition system") into thinking ordinary people were celebrities, potentially allowing one person to impersonate another. In 2017 researchers added stickers to [stop signs](/wiki/Stop_sign "Stop sign") and caused an ANN to misclassify them.[[289]](#cite_note-:4-289)

ANNs can however be further trained to detect attempts at [deception](/wiki/Deception "Deception"), potentially leading attackers and defenders into an arms race similar to the kind that already defines the [malware](/wiki/Malware "Malware") defense industry. ANNs have been trained to defeat ANN-based anti-[malware](/wiki/Malware "Malware") software by repeatedly attacking a defense with malware that was continually altered by a [genetic algorithm](/wiki/Genetic_algorithm "Genetic algorithm") until it tricked the anti-malware while retaining its ability to damage the target.[[289]](#cite_note-:4-289)

In 2016, another group demonstrated that certain sounds could make the [Google Now](/wiki/Google_Now "Google Now") voice command system open a particular web address, and hypothesized that this could "serve as a stepping stone for further attacks (e.g., opening a web page hosting drive-by malware)".[[289]](#cite_note-:4-289)

In "[data poisoning](/wiki/Adversarial_machine_learning#Data_poisoning "Adversarial machine learning")", false data is continually smuggled into a machine learning system's training set to prevent it from achieving mastery.[[289]](#cite_note-:4-289)

### Data collection ethics

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Deep_learning&action=edit&section=39 "Edit section: Data collection ethics")]

The deep learning systems that are trained using supervised learning often rely on data that is created or annotated by humans, or both.[[291]](#cite_note-291) It has been argued that not only low-paid [clickwork](/wiki/Clickworkers "Clickworkers") (such as on [Amazon Mechanical Turk](/wiki/Amazon_Mechanical_Turk "Amazon Mechanical Turk")) is regularly deployed for this purpose, but also implicit forms of human [microwork](/wiki/Microwork "Microwork") that are often not recognized as such.[[292]](#cite_note-:13-292) The philosopher [Rainer Mühlhoff](/wiki/Rainer_M%C3%BChlhoff "Rainer Mühlhoff") distinguishes five types of "machinic capture" of human microwork to generate training data: (1) [gamification](/wiki/Gamification "Gamification") (the embedding of annotation or computation tasks in the flow of a game), (2) "trapping and tracking" (e.g. [CAPTCHAs](/wiki/CAPTCHA "CAPTCHA") for image recognition or click-tracking on Google [search results pages](/wiki/Search_engine_results_page "Search engine results page")), (3) exploitation of social motivations (e.g. [tagging faces](/wiki/Tag_(Facebook) "Tag (Facebook)") on [Facebook](/wiki/Facebook "Facebook") to obtain labeled facial images), (4) [information mining](/wiki/Information_mining "Information mining") (e.g. by leveraging [quantified-self](/wiki/Quantified_self "Quantified self") devices such as [activity trackers](/wiki/Activity_tracker "Activity tracker")) and (5) [clickwork](/wiki/Clickworkers "Clickworkers").[[292]](#cite_note-:13-292)

# What is deep learning?

[Artificial Intelligence](https://www.ibm.com/think/artificial-intelligence)

17 June 2024

Link copied

## Authors

[Jim Holdsworth](https://www.ibm.com/think/author/jim-holdsworth) 

Staff Writer

IBM Think

[Mark Scapicchio](https://www.ibm.com/think/author/Mark-Scapicchio) 

Editor, Topics & Insights

IBM Think

## What is deep learning?

Deep learning is a subset of [machine learning](https://www.ibm.com/think/topics/machine-learning?) that uses multilayered [neural networks](https://www.ibm.com/think/topics/neural-networks?), called deep neural networks, to simulate the complex decision-making power of the human brain. Some form of deep learning powers most of the [artificial intelligence (AI)](https://www.ibm.com/think/topics/artificial-intelligence?) applications in our lives today.

The chief difference between deep learning and machine learning is the structure of the underlying neural network architecture. “Nondeep,” [traditional machine learning](https://www.ibm.com/think/topics/machine-learning-types) models use simple neural networks with one or two computational layers. Deep learning models use three or more layers, but typically hundreds or thousands of layers to train the models.

While [supervised learning](https://www.ibm.com/think/topics/supervised-learning) models require structured, labeled input data to make accurate outputs, deep learning models can use [unsupervised learning](https://www.ibm.com/think/topics/unsupervised-learning). With unsupervised learning, deep learning models can extract the characteristics, features and relationships they need to make accurate outputs from raw, unstructured data. Additionally, these models can even evaluate and refine their outputs for increased precision.

Deep learning is an aspect of data science that drives many applications and services that improve [automation](https://www.ibm.com/consulting/automation), performing analytical and physical tasks without human intervention. This enables many everyday products and services, such as digital assistants, voice-enabled TV remotes, credit card [fraud detection](https://www.ibm.com/think/topics/fraud-detection), self-driving cars and generative AI.
